TFIE DAISY'S "How glad and gay the meadows, How still and blue the sky ! How sweet to live here always. And never, never die !" So thought a great white daisy, When through the meadow-land A heedless lad came whistling. With willow switch in hand. It snapped her stalk so slender. And flung her to the ground. While all her fair companions In silent grief hung round. One violet held a teardrop Within her eye of blue. Although you might have fancied ''Twas bot 4 bead of dew; A hyacinth bent o'er her, A kingcup shook his head; The tender lark that loved her Would fain hafve died instead. Then, presently a rustling, 'The wind came sweeping by; It lifted up poor daisy With something like a sigh, And dropped her in the streamlet That ran past rush and reed. For, oh, the sun was scorching. And she was faint indeed. Now like a star she floated, And now she all but sank. Until at last she rested Upon the mossy bank. There stood a painter's canvas. And on it, plain as plain, The-sky, the trees, the water, All nature lived again. The painter glanced around lan., The daisy pleased his eve; He put her in his picture, she might never die!. ,--Little Folks.

Tallevrand acknowledged a pathetic letter from a lady friend announcing her widowhood with. a note of two words," He was, madame !" And when the easily con. soled dame wrote. nnt very long afterwards, soliciting his influence in behalf of an officer she was about to marry, he merely replied, "Ho, ho, madame !" More satisfactosy to the recipient was Lord Eldon's note to his friend 'Dr. Fisl,er, of the Charterhouse:—" Dear Fisher,-1 Cannot. to-day, give you the tpreferment for which you .as.—Your sincere friend, Eldon. (Turn over.) I gave it you yesterday." It is said that on one occasion, as Miss Wordsworth sister of the tpoet, was passing through a Wood which the stockdone was filling with its soft music,she fell in with a country-Woman, who exclaimed, " Am so fond of stockdoveg.." "Oh thought Miss Wordsworth, "at last I have come on one of Nature's poets, with a soul to appreciate the ,Iseautif ul music of the birds." Xery ruth- leeslv was theAream disenchanted by an explanatory re- mark of tie woman's—" Some likes them 141 , pies, and some likes hem roasted; but fsr my part, I think there's nothing like them-stewed with onions !" Wonderfully .convenient sa the teleplicne un- doubtedly is, the invention is not without its dangers and its drawbacks. Terrible things have occurred from its careless edse by persons in- sufficiently versed in its ways and workings. To give an example: a lady a akortitime ago received an invitation by telephone to dine in the country. Tam- ping away from the instrument, . she asked her husband ..what (archly excuse she could send-this time. Through the telephone with awidl. distinct Less came back the answer: "It you don't want to come, you needn't Send any excuse at all." Alas! she had been unaware that "asides" not spoken directly into the instrument were often audible at the other end.

Experience is a great teacher, and m.y experience as a father has taught me a real lively rollicking boy or a self-willed imperious little miss of four or five summers can completely destroy and set at naught many of one's most beautiful theories regarding the rearing of chit- dren. 43ut it is comforting to feel that about half of your theories ought really tote upset anyhow, and you realise how much more charming children-really are as ,ditldren than they would be ,as the little ladies and gentlemen" of your imagination. I don't want him to -know it, but the very willfulness and defiance of my authority, by the little tow-head of three years cuddled up in his bed upstairs is irresistibly fanny sometimes— the little rascal. WHY .PICNIQO AR& SO-CALLED.—Everybody knows what pieuic is, but most folk would find it hard to say how it got that name, and yet it is simple ensugh when you Come to learn it. When a picnic was being arranged for, the .custom originally‘was that those who intended to be present should supply the eatables and drinkables. A list of those necessaries having been drawn up, it was passed round, and each person picked out the article that he or she was willing to furnish, and the name of the article was Ricked, or ticked off the list. The open-air entertainment thus became known as a ' pick and nick.' The custom is said to date from 1802. so that the picnic is wholly an institution of the nineteenth century. As started, it must ,have strongly resembled what is now failed a "surprise part7.".--Littlf Fear,

Surgeon ?eke, who next to 3,1 T. Stanley is.the hero of the hour, is an Irishman.

Mr. If. 3L Stanley has been elected a temporary member of the National Liberal Club. The same privilege has just been extended to Mr. P. Abigail, M.P., of Sydney, New South Wales, the lion. I. Lynch, senator of the United States, the lion. Robert Adams, of New York, and the Indian National Congress delegate, Mr. Nath. Sobrentra Bantierjee.

At the conclusion of his address at the Albert Hall on Monday, Mr. Stanley referred to the fact that he had acquired thousands of miles of new territories for England. As a matter of fact, he made treaties all along his route from -Lake Albert, and these treaties are lodged at the Foreign Office. There can be little cioubt that Lord Safi:Wiry will support Mr. Stanley'section, and so put annild to all pos-ibbity of Germany pushing northwards behind the British sphere.

The accounts received from Windsor Castle indi- cate how greatly interested the Queen was in Mr. Stanley's brief lecture on Tuesday night. The pre- sente,ufiSir Francis De Winton, Sir Wm. IFKinnon, Lord .Knutsford, and. Lordalisbury gave to the royal dinner party and the little gathering which followed a strong coloniallifavour, and it is stated that Her Majesty not only showed marked interest in Mr. Stanley's discoveries;but betrayed something like,witeen anxiety tci know-ell that could be learnt respecting the doings and eopirations of the Ger- mans in East Africa.

The Queen intends to visit Edinburgh during the last week in August, when on her way from Osberne to Balmoral. Her Majesty will probably reside at Holyrood Palace for three days, in order that she may have time to inspect both the exhibi- tion and the Forth Bridge, and she wilj pay a visit to the *Duke and Duchess Izif Buccleuch at Dalkeith Palace during her stay.

From Paris comes the information that an essen- tial to a perfect dinner service at the present time is a small mirror, handsdruely mounted, placed upon the table in front of each lady. This singular ap- purtenance enables the lady to gratify her natural solicitude as to the condition of her coiffure and as to her general appearance; furthermore, by an adroit, manipulation of the mirror one is able to see what is going on around her.

The Museum of Antiquities at Gottingen has just madela remarkable addition to its treasures. It consists in nothing less than the battered door of the tUniversity prison, on,which is cut in bold char- &eters. the name of "Bismarck." It seems that the ex-Chancellor, in his law-student days, suffered a briefperiod of detention there for some trifling breach of discipline, and amused himself by carving his patronymic with unmistakable clearness on the door of the cell.

The 'National Physical Recreation Society,of which Mr. Herbert Gladstone is president, is organising a gymnastic fate at the Agricultural Hall, Islington, which will occupy all the evenings of Whit-week. Is this body was established for the promotion of physical recreation among the working classes, the programme will be sufficiently varied to attract all sections of them, including, boxing, quarter-staff play, pole jumping, and football.

Schulz writes :—" To the list of English- men who speak French well enough to address a public meeting, the name of Mr. Cunninghame Grs.hean might well be added,as any one who heard his short address in that language to the foreign waiters, in Hyde Park on Sunday afternoon can testify. Mr. Graham achieved a much greater lingiaistill feat last year at the Workmen's Confer- ence in Paris, where he not only made a speech in Frenck. but translated the speeches of the Spanish delegates into French."

You will have heard from other witnesses of the great &access of Sunday's demonstratimi in favour of the eight hours day. Perfect order was main- tained. The weather was fine, but not too hot; immense crowds turned out; the bands played well; and them; was a capital display of appropriate banners. As the demonstrators were returning from Ilyda Park, and were marching along Buck- ingham alace-road, towards Westminster Bridge. they Met Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone walking towards Belgravia. The Liberal leader was enthusiastically cheered along the whole line of the procession.

The Berlin censorship, like other censorships' has curious ways. Its latest exploit says Mr. Smalley, id the " New York Tribune,' is to alter for the benefit of the non-German world, Prince Bismarck's message of thanks to the three or four thousand people who lately telegraphed him their sym- pathies. "On the occasion of my dismissal," said the Prince. ,In the Reuter version " dismissal" is toned down-to" resignation," presumably in obedi- ence to orders from, a high quarter. Mr. Lowe, of the "Times,".is my :authority ; and he is none too friendly to Prince liismarck, though he wrote his Life, a very good Life, in two large volumes.

American Senators and State Representatives stick like limpets to the title of" Honourable"; so do their " ladiee who have married into any titled family in Europe, and English officials are mighty tenacious of all that is due to them. The present Master of the Rolls wrote himself down in the visitors' list in a foreign hotel, thus :—" Sir William Baliol Brett, Baron Esher, Pair Anglais, Premier Juge de la Cour (le Cessation de Sa Majeso la Reine d'Angleterre." Gn the other band, the late Dake of Rutland, who was there about the same time, in- scribed himself simply by a signature that looked like an "R," a clash, and a " D.'

The levee on Tuesday was unusually crowded. So great was the pressure of visitor. 3 to Cour that a large sahon near the top of the staircase at St. ilames's Palace was opened for the occasion and need as a waiting-room for those who were for the time unable to force their way into the state apartments. Lord SaliSbury looked jaded and inexpressibly bored by the obligation .of remaining after he had made his bow in what is termed "thtweneral circle" —that is, the group of high offlcialsodomvtic and foreign, who stand in the Throne-room facing the Royal 14'aznily. Lord Spencer, Lord Kimberley, and Sir William Harcourt went through the rooms together.

Ernest Renan, the religious historian and critic, has charming quarters at the College de France, of which he is rector. His rooms are lit throughout with the electric light, conveyed from tile college laboratory, and they are furnished with both taste and luxury. Reran is getting to he as stout as the typical medimval abbot, and for the same reason— ;eve of good cheer. Madame Renan, a daughter, by the way, of Ary Sebeffer, the painter, is a remark- ably good cook, and her pride is to tickle Renan's palate every day with come cunningly-devised dish, Ben.= has a heavy sensual face, with not a little of the Jew in it, although he has not a trace of Judaism in his blood, Bight centuries 0 Brawl life

" Bi gew, Spinner," said Roger, ." tha'rt blessed wi' a witty wife Aw,could'nd ha' gi'en ;Peggy a better lesson aw'd studied for attionth.' "Nor me ayther," said Bill o' mi Granny's " hoo's cured her o' stomaeh-warch fora bit." "Well, hoo'll nod ,Colne Wi"t to eawr heawse ageeon, heaw't be," eaid Spinner Dick ; "id suited me gradely weel. Avellbet boo goes nowheer a- spongin' for a week er two. No deawt hoo'll ged o'er id, an' startspongin' ageeon, after a bit, but id'll nod be at eawr heawse, forth' wife says hoo'll serve her as ill ageeon th fest time boo does coma:" "iIOO'S th' reet oti't," said Young Turpin. "If boo cornd .mek a lastin' cure, boo can cure her for a time, same as me an' Billy Robi'son dud wi' Owd Skinflint h is-sel'." " Wod dud yo care th' owd chap on, like" in- quired Roger. "We cured him o' thad sgeet, him his nickname," replied Turpin, "an' geet him i' th' humour for givin' us some'at." " Givin' To some'at, l" exclaimed Bill o' mi Granny's, with a look of surprise, "heaw the derry wer thad ? Aw oe'er knew him to give owt mi life."

"Thad wer just wod aw-said to Billy Robi'son, when we wer' talkin' o'er him one fleet," said Turin. "Aw dornd know beaw id coom onto th' carpet gradely ; but some way, two or three on us geet agate chattin' o'er Skinflint an' t' Wife. They , live aside o' us. yo' know ; an' they'd just bin killite a pig. Bill Robi'son said he .wondered whether they'd give onybotly a bit, same as owd-fashioned ' nebbers (neighbours) used to do. 'Nod they,' aw said, they'll part wi' nowt, mon. Aw'll bet they I begrudge every bit o' smook as gooas up their kit- ellen chimbley, an' iliey wodn'd. part wi' thad if they waurn'd feeard o' bein!_stified wi' 't%'" "By gum," said Billy," but aw could like a bit o' nice bacon, cheeap. An' avell Just see if aw cornd gad a bit eawt on 'ern, too.' Aw said he'd be sucked in if he tried, but at last ,he managed to drag me into th' "lark;" an' we waited till th' owd couple had just gone to bed, an' then geet ready for action. Billy fotched his !pin eawt ; showed nio where th' pig hed bin put—into a little place at back o' th' heawse, an' under th' owd fooak's room window; an' towd mo that when he fired aw wer to run deawn t' looan. an mek as big a clatter as aw could, so as to imitate some thieves runnin' away. Well, aw acted up to mi orders, an' th' job warked weel., " In a bit, Billy tired, once,twice, three times ! an' Off aw seet deawn t' Moan; rnAckin as mulch din as 'hofe a dozen chaps. Well, Billy hed hardly fired th' last shot afoor th' room window wer shot up, an owd Skinflint appeared. "Whoever are yo, an' wod dun yo *ant here at this time o' th' fleet?" he sheawted.

"Bh, is thad yo, William," little Billy sheawts back, avv'm fairly fain yo've wakkened. Aw wer just pas.sin', wi' th' gun o'er my shoother, an' by gum, aw spied two little thievin' divvles wer after geddhe at yore pig inside here !" "Laws o' mercy !" said owd Peggy. for hoo'd get., ten to th' winclew, too, " we's be mordered next. Heor yo, William, heaw they're runnin'." "Aye, said owd Bill, " I hear 'em." "0, yo may rest yoresels content," said Billy Robi'son, "They'll come nooan back, nod they." " Dornd yo think sooa ?" said Peggy. " Nowe, aw dornd think they will," said owd gkinflint, "an' aw thank tha, Billy, wi' o my heart, for thi plucky wark. Awl' co an' si' th' motain'."

A case of considerable interest to medical men has just been recorded by a French surgeon. A man in January last, while temporarily demented, swal- lowed a teaspoon. Eighteen days afterwards he applied for relief at the hospital in consequence of the intense pain caused by the spoon. On examin- ation externally nothing could be felt, and doubt was expressed whether alter all anything abnormal had been swallowed. As, however, some in was experienced when pressure was applied to the region of the stomach the surgeon Aetermined to, investigate further. With this object in view he' employed an electric exploring instrument. No sooner had the latter passed into the stomach than the tinkle of an electric bell emphatically proved that ametallic substance had ,been -struck by the exploring apparatus. The usual =operation wras then proceeded with, the teaspoon was founthand extracted, and the patient left the hospital at the end of two months perfectly convalescent.

CHAPTER XVIII. PEEL‘NO A POILTENT. "WllO is this?" exclaimed Mark, sharply. , "It is I, Mark," replied Ruth, in a tremblierg voice. "And what are you doing here?" There was a pause for a few moments before the girl spoke. "I could not sleep," she faltered. Mark's voice eras very stern and harsh when he spoke again. " Tell me," he said, "had you made an appoint- ment to meet Martin here after we were all in bed ?" No, oh no, Mark," she cried, eagerly. "Then why are you here?" he said, harshly. There was wain a few moments' silence, when she said firmly, just as she was sinking fast in the estima- tion cif the man who loved her, and who had placed her upon a ,pinnacle so very high above all women be lmew— " I saw how angry you were with Martin, and I was afraid that he would be unprepared to meet you. I I thought, too, that you had fastened the door, and I came to listen, and then to —" "Sit up for, and let him in:" said Mark, harshly. " Yes, Mark," she said, ins low voice. " Ruth," he exclaimed, angrily—and there was some thing very repellent in hes voice—" you are a mother- less girl, and it is for your sake that Miss Klopstock resides with us. Do you think she would approve of such ma act as this ?" " No, Mark," she said, her voice trembling sa she spoke. "You have not been to bed ?" "No, Mark." "Go then at once." 'he exclaimed. "Ruth, I did not think you could have been so unmaidenly—so unwise."

" Mark!" she said -softly; and there was gentle reproof and appeal mingled in her voice as she spoke; but he was sternness itself now. "Go at once," he said, harshly; and, with a low sigh, she crept up the stairs, and he listened until he heard .her door softly close. Mark waited for a few minutes, and then going to the front door, he opened it, stepped out, and walked .sharply away. The brisk night air came cool and refreshing to his • cheek, but it did not chase away the strange humour of his brain. Something was going to happen he felt sure, and now it took the form that that was some troubleat the great office. "Yes, I thought as much," he exclaimed, for just then he heard the loud rattle of wheels and the _gallop- • ing of hoofs upon the stones. He was too old a Londoner not to know what that meant, and, as a fire - engine dashed by, he ran after it with all his might, wondering that he should have bud such ,a warning of the coming danger, and keeping up his rapid career till he was obliged to stop and recover his breath. "1 must go to a doctor's," he exclaimed, impatiently. "My nerves seem regularly shattered. I see a fire- engine, and I immediately jump at conclusions that our place is in a blaze, and poor old Klopstoak beitig frizzled. The engine has gone quite a different way." He walked on, feeling relieved. " Know where the fire is, constable ?" "Over the Surrey side, sir Lambeth way, I "Thanks," said .lark; and then to himself, "I wish all the other phantoms my brain conjures up would dissolve as readily." put they would not, and as he walked on at -frown ,settled upon his forehead as he thought of Ruth's behaviour tha^ night, and a faint ray of hopefulness • that after all she might not care for his brother-seemed to be crushed out for ever. He had been veining Cityward for sometime, when he hesitated as to whether he should go any further. 'The sharp exercise had given him the relief 138 ro-eded, sending his sluggish blood dancing through his "seine, ;and making his brain clearer and brighter than it had >felt since morning. "I'll go all the way," he said, "as I've come solar. I wonder how poor old Klopstock is ?" The streets were almost deserted as he strode along, 'with the long rows of gas lamps running before him, seeming to meet far ahead, like 60 many bright beads -on a black ground. Now and then a hansom rattled .noisily by, the empty streets echoing to its wheel', -while every now and then he came upon a tipsy 'wanderer or some unfortunate homeless creature ',asleep in the corner of a doorway. Now and then he passed a policeman in one of the -City streets, going slowly from door to door, and -shutter to shutter, to try if all was fast, and turn his light down one or other of the narrow business courts '.npon his beat. "There," thought Mark, "I need not be anxious about our place with these men always on the look -out. I'll go and Bee the light in the old fellow's window, though, before Igo back. Good night, .eonstable." "Goad night, sir," was the reply. He walked on, turned out of the grim deserted etreet, and down the narrow lane, to stop at length before the great, red brick, old-fashioned building, with its solid doors, iron railings in front, and heavy grating, that was never closed, at the entrance to the archway over the court at the side. Humphreys' establishment had once been the resi- dence of some City magnate in the good old times when the City prinees did not live out of town, but marched in procession with their families on Sundays to one or other of the great forsaken churches, where sermons are now preached to congregations of half a dozen or so, including the pew-opener and the clerk. "I wish I could get over these old womanish feel- ings," cried Mark. "I declare it is ridiculous. If I am like this at five- and-thirty, what shall I be at laity r There was a light burning in the entry as usual. That was all right. There was another light in the long counting-house, shining down as he could see through a gauze blind, bearing the word " Humphreys " in gilt letters that once were bright, and this light was glistening faintly on the old mshogany desks and brass rails. That was all right, too. It was kept burning all night, so that when the policeman on the beat came round, he could look in and see that the place was safe. There was yet another light burning on the first door over the entrance. That was all right, too, for it was In Mr. Klopstock's room, where he slept in com- pany with a brace of pistols and an old-fashioned brass blunderbuss with a bell mouth, all of which were supposed to be loaded as they hung on nails over the chimney piece; but when they were loaded no one knew' nor yet when they had been cleaned. In fact, the flint had tumbled out of the lock of one of the pistols, and had been picked up by the woman who acted as housekeeper, and placed for safety in the mouth of the blunderbuss, ready to make a horrible wound in some burglar's breast if the aforesaid weapon could have been fired, which was not in the slightest degree probable; and really, if it bad been discharged, the probabilities were that the place facing the muzzle would have been safer tkaan !Anywhere near the butt. , A/ Mark Woolford looked up he could see the glimmer of the lamp shining through the blinds, and, with a sigh of satisfaction, he mentally declared that after all he was glad he Came down, if it was only to I find that his old friend was apparently sleeping /*awfully. • "I don't think it would be a bad plan to have this old gateway repaired and used," he said to himself, as he croosed the roadway, and went down the narrilev passage under the archway, leading to aside entrance, and to some ware rooms; "butt don't know: any evil- disposed person would find a way of getting it open if required, and the gas and the police are the real safe- ; guards. All the same, though, he thought of the large ' amount lying that night in Mr. Middlecombe's strong vault, along with valuable convertible securities that were worth a very serieus amount. "If any one could get at them," he said half aloud, as if an.wering his thoughts. He went down the court, and tried the side door, } which was, as he expected it to be, perfectly fast. Then he looked up the side of the great building, to where the stars gleamed down; then along the court. All was perfectly still, even to solemnify, and, with a sigh of relief, he was about to turn and walk out into the street, when there was a sudden flash of light right in his eyes, and a gruff voice exclaimed: "What now?"

MR. STANLEY IN LONDON.

On Saturday eveiing Mr. Stanley was entertained at dinner by Mr. O. L. Stephen, at his picturesque house Cadogan-squixe. Among those invited to meet the great explorer were the Earl of Limerick, Profesmr Vara- bery, Sir William Mackinnon, Sir Arnold Kemball, Sir Peter Lumsdan, Mr. Lucas, Mr. Edward Lawson, Mr. Francis Jeutre, General Brackenbury, Dr. W. H. Russell, and Sir Thatnas Sanderson. In the evening there was a crow ded reception. RECEPTION BY THE ROYAL GEOGRAPHICAL

div.head: SOCIETY.
div.p: SOCIETY.

A magnificent reception was given by the members of the Royal Geographical Society and their ifriends to Mr. Stanley, in the Royal Albert Hall, London, on Monday night. The gigantic build- ing was crowded in every part, except those incon- venient corners near the organ, whence nothing could be seen. Of course, in the immense rotunda the vast majority of the people pre'sent could hear nething intelligibly. All that reached them was the sound of Mr. Stanley's voice, without its articulation. But they saw him, and this was ' their main purpose; and each of them had a hand map of his travels, besides the assistance of an '4mmense chart, stretched across the front of the organ. Amongst those present were the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke and Duchess of Teelt, the Princess Victoria of Tuck. the Duke of Cambridge the Princess and Prince Victor of Hohenlohe, the :Duke of Fife, and a distinguished company, including several foreign Ministers, and M. Ifeles Leclercy (president of the Brussels Geographical Society), M. Beltran° (delegate of the Geogrephical Society of Geneva), &c. Mr. Stanley was led into the hail ial a sort of tri- umphal procession, headed by the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Edinburgh, the great explorer walking next, side by side with the President, Sir Mount-Stewart Grant Duff. Then came Mr. Stan- ley's fellow travellers—Dr. Parke, Mr. Mountjoy Jephson, Captain Nelson, and Lieutenant airs— escorted by other officials of the society. The -vast gathering of people at once rose to their !feet and broke forth into applause. When the brave band had crossed the arena and takeis their place on the platform, and a full view was got of them, and especially of their intrepid leadcr,the cheers became vehement. A more animated and :splendid scene it would be difficult to imagine. The proceedings were begun withont delay. " The President declared hhis to be the .lanzest gathering' ever held under the auspices •of .the society,and proceeded to sketch the romantic career 'of Mr. Stanley prier to his last great journey, and to make some references to the dangers and difficulties Nyhich had marked his latest 'exploit. He did jus- tice also to the immense services performed by him and his companions to the cause of geographical science. Mr. Stanley, who wore the medal of the society, then rose to address the assembly, this being the signal; for a renewed burst of cheering. Proceeding, Mr. Stanley re- minded his hearers that his journey across Afrioa was 6,000 miles in length, and occupied '987 days, for a con- siderable portion of which it lay through the great:forest. Of this Mr. Stanley went on to speak, after -quotingwhat he characterised as a somewhat inadequate description. Nyassa Land was not Africa butitself,he said. The for- est's greatest length was 621. English miles, he greatest , width 517 miles. It made a compact square area of , 321,057 square miles. A serpentine line drawn through this district would represent the route of the expedition, a description a which the speaker went on to give in impressive and graphic language. First of all • he dwelt upon the unimaginable wealth of 'vegeta- tion, absolutely impenetrable to sunshine. -Generally the light was a misty twilight, and at times it was tin- possible to read a book, although to the outside world it was day. When it rained the water poured down for 12, 15, and 18 hours, until the travellers wondered

whether they were never to see dry ground again. At night the stillness was oppressive, but now andtheu they would be wakened fermi their slumbers by the Sailing of a tree, which made the earth quake. He described the enormous size of the forest giants, and the density with which they cover the ground. He calculated that the forest covered 224 million acres, and allowing to each tree 30 feet round and only 48 to the acre, they had 10,752 millions of trees. He next described the fauna of the forest, and then came to the race of pigmies whom he had encountered. These he considered the only peop e on the globe—the only people now inhabiting it— who, from primeval times, had never removed ,from their homes, and like the giant trees of their native for- ests, seeming to defy time and fate. He ascribed to them great natural intelligence, ready appreciation of affection and kindness, and much ingenuity in conversing by means of signs. In these des- riptions Mr. Stanley gave rein to his powers of humoristic narrative, and caused many a ripple of laughter to flow over the hall by his quaint comparisons. Having finished with the great forest, Mr. Stanley next described the open or pasture country an I the races that inhabit it. He described the anthropological distinctions of these, and the character of their villages and their modes of life. Then he passed on to the interesting dis- coveries he had made in connection with the Lake Aibert Edward, the mountains of the moon, and the extension _ .

of the Lake Victoria to the south-west. He pointed out the effect of the River Semleka, between Lake Albert Edward and Lake Albert Nyanza, and ventured to prophesy that by the year 2150 there would be no Lake Albert Edward and in a short time after there would be no Lake Albert Nyanza. Dealing fipther with the Moun- tains of the Moon, he spoke of a legend concerning thin he had heard in Cairo, and used it as a text upon which to found a few well-chosen sentences concerning the dis- covery, that in the snow-tops of the mountains was the source of the Nile sotyital to the people of Egypt After completing his description of the region, Mr. Stanley said the question had often been asked by stolid, thoughtful people, what good had been derived from this expedition, Which less than a year ago was about commencing its long march to the sea. He said to humanity the gain had been great. The ,world was richer by the knowledge that there were ten million more trees than they knew of before in the world; that there were inexhaustible stores of rubbers, gums, and vege- table nuts; that there was navigation by which those interested in these treasures could proceed to collect them ; and that in those vegetable products millions of degraded human beings within that great forest would in process of time find that they had something of far vas- ter value than the flesh of their fellow-creatures. (Cheers.) As a Christian nation we ought to rejoice that by the few thousands of pounds we lent to the ser- vice we had rescued over 400 men, women, and children from slavery, had restored 200 to their homes in Egypt, had delivered the late governor from a stagnant state of impossibilities to the active service of a friendly nation, and had restored a gallant Italian explorer to his native country, and a Greek merchant to his family. He (Mr. Stanley) was qiiite sure that we begrudged our money as little as he and his companions did their services. As geographers, the society must be gratified by the wide ex- tension of geographical knowledge gained. The Aruwimi river was now known throughout almost its entire length. They knew of the existence of the great forest, and the connection between the great lakes: the Nile had been traced to its fountainhead. The lofty mountains of the Moon, known since Homer's time, had now been surveyed and located. The best portions of Africa had now been traversed and described. There was no exaggeration in the assertion that every mile traversed by his expedition would serve in theconiina time to extend British com- merce and stimulate 13r?tish enterprise and industry. (Cheers.) Finally, they had extended British possessions to the Eastern limits pt he Congo, adding to them thous- ands of square miles without force of arms, but by other and more potent considerations. (Cheers.) Their pro- mise had been on setting out on this expedition to do as little harm and as much good as possible. He therefore submitted this bare outline of their services in the hope that they would be acceptable. (Long and continued cheering.) At the close of this address, which lasted an hour,

The Prince of Wales moved a vote of thanks. He spoke of the value and interest of the address, and said Mr. Stanley's name would go down to posterity as that of one of our greatest travellers and philanthropists. (Cheers.) The resolution was then put to the meeting, and car- ried amidst acclamation.

The President, rising said that in the year 1873 the Royal Geographical Society assigned its gold medal •to Mr. Stanley, by doing which it exhausted all its ordi- nary powers of distinction. The council of the society had come to the conclusion that Mr. Stanley had done so much more since that time that it was their duty to as- sign him another medal. (Cheers.) Ms. Stanley could not have wished, and they could not have wished, that the honour should appertain only to him. The society had accordingly awarded a medal to all his companions. (Loud cheers.) The Stanley medal was made of British gold, which had been given for the express purpose by Mr. Pritchard Morgan, M.P. (Cheers.) The Prince of Wakes then made the presentation to Mr. Stanley and his companions in the following order : Lieutenant Stairs, Dr. Parke, Captain Nelson, Mr. Jeph- son, and Mr. Bonny. All were cordially greeted, and Mr. Stanley acknowledged the compliments. The President expressed the thanks of the meeting to the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Edinburgh, and the proceedings then terminated.
A summary of the accounts has been issued under the failure of the Hon. Charles Henry George Cadogan, youngest son of the late Earl Cadogan. His debts are returned at £1,871, and be has no assets.

div.head: CHAPTER XIX.
div.p: CHAPTER XIX.

SAMSON IS REINSTALLED. JoY had not pervaded the residence at Bow since Mr. Samson Hall had returned home late in the afternoon of the day when Mark had sent him back. Days bad passed, and he had not been forgiven. Mrs. Hall had been with three humble apologies to Mark Woolford, and she had seen him. They had conversed together, aad in a quiet way Mark had drawn from the poor little woman an account of her Bufforings. " When he is all right, sir, the best of husbands;

bat when he forgets himself,- and gets to the drink, sir, it's very dreadful indeed." "And so all this account we have had from time to time about Hall's fits has been a fiction ? " "Well, sir," sobbed the poor woman, " it is fits." "Of drunkenness?" " Ye—es, sir; but he always is very ill." "And you have screened his follies by false- hoods?" "Please, sir," said the little woman, humbly, " am his wife, and his wages here, sir, are of conga quenee. You wouldn't have me expose him?" "No," said Mark. "You won't discharge him, please, sir?" she sobbed. "I don't know what to say, Mrs. Hall," said Mark. "Such a man is not fit for a responsible post. Hon am I to trust a drunkard ?" "Please, sir, we are none of us perfect," said the pcea little woman, humbly. Mark winced, for the face of his brother seemed to tome up before him. " No," he said; " we are none of us perfect." "I'll promise for him, sir, that he'll never do so any more." "Why, yeti foolish little woman," said Mark, smiling, "I'll be bound to say that when heis drinking, he pays no heed to you." " Nota bit, sir," she sobbed, ingenuously; "and I dc try so very hard to keep him straight, and over and ores again, when I have had him so, I have hid his -,ilothes so that:oe shouldn't get up and came to the office." Markt looked at her searchingly, but she was Ter: easy to read, and he could see that she "as psrfectly genuine at heart—ano-her of that large band of struggling women always ready to stand between a weak husband and the consequences of his folly. "Well, Mrs. Hall," he said, "I have Seen you as you wished, and heard what you have to say. Now go back, and tell Samson Hall that I consider hi J con- duct disgraceful, and that, in Mr. Klopstock's absence, -I have decided to suspend him." "Oh, sir," she sobbed, "isn't this very, very hard ? " " Not at all," said Mark, smiling " Now -I'm going to take you into My confidence. I don't want to ruin your husbancil but to give him a severe lesson. Let him believe that be is discbarged, and by and by, when he is really repentant, I will take him on." •" Oh, thank you—thank you, sir." "And meantime," said Mark, "you can come ,quietly, toed draw his wives." "Oh, heaven bless—" "-Stop!" said Mark, "only on one condition." "I'll promise anything, sir." "Then promise me that he is not told of this; at all events not for sometime," "Oh, yes, sir. I promise you," cried the poor woman,joyfully; "and he said that you were such a hard, cruel man." "So I am," said Mark, quietly. "There, Mrs. Hall, now go, please, and mind this is a profound secret. Before he could stay her, the grateful little woman had caught his hand in hers, and kissed it, and then hurried tearfully away. But though there was joy in her heart, and the fire of gratitude burned warmly, poor little Mrs. Hall's hours I at home were not very pleasant. On hearing that he was not to go back, Samson Hall, instead of becoming repentant and mild, filled the atmosphere full of bad language, and fulminated furi- ously against Mark Woolford and his brother. "I know 'em both,' he cried in hisdrunken passion. "I know how young Martin's been let off ten times as bad things as ever rve done, and how he's carrying on now. Missus." "Yes, dear." "I'll pull 'em both down, that I wida" "No, no, dear, you'll ,try and not offend again, and perhaps some day —' " Hang some day!" cried the porter, furiously. "Only just wait till old Klop gets better, and I'll let 'em see." This was repeated ad infinitum, till Mrs. Hall began to wonder whether she had not better go and see Mr. Woolford, and tell him how badly his moral medicine worked. Still she waited and hoped on till, upon that evening when Mark had suffered from so severe a fit of uneasiness, it might almost lisle been caused by some kind of psychic influence, for, just when he was most uneasy, Samson Hall had been vowing the direst revenge upon the scoundr,l of a stuck-up chief clerk, who was robbing an honest man of his bread. He was perfectly sober, for the simple reason that he had had no money to obtain drink; and he was, with his shivering little wife for audience, just saying for the hundredth t:me that he would ruin the Wool- fords as soon as old Klop was better, when there was a sharp knock at the door. "Hush! for goodness sake," cried Mrs. Hall, rising from the late tea they were having—a meal made fes- tive with a couple of toasted bloaters—and going to the door to return with a larawn envelope of the regular telegram pattern. "Oh, dear," she cried, trembling; "I hope nobody's dying or dead." Rather a futile wish, by the way, but unnoticed by her husband, who snatched the missive from her hands, tore it open, and read aloud: From Klopstock, St. Mary-lane, to S. Hall, Sona- bird-lane, Bow: "Come on here directly. Edwards is out. You will stay all night." "Oh, Sam, what does that mean?" exclaimed the little woman. "Mean, woman? Victory. Old Klop has come to the conclusion that the Woolfords are a had lot, kicked them out, and sent for me to come back." • "But you will be careful, Sam. Please—pray don't touch a drop on the way.' " Bahl" "Pray don't, Sam. You know what you are if you have one glass." '• Yah I" "You are never happy until you have had more." " Tchah! Give me a shilling." "If you lose this chance, Sam, you may never—" Bang! That a as the front door shut loudly and quickly upon I Mr. Samson Hall's _retiring form; still not BO quickly but that it admitted a strong smell of gas from the I neighbouring works; and to show how fond he was of his wife's advice, he went to the public-house at the corner --Oh! those awkward corners, how men cld run up against them !—and had one glass before mounting the 'bus, taking another when be got off, and then going saraight to the office to be admitted by the house- keeper. "Mr. Klopstock wants to see me directly," he said, with a tone of importance in his voice. "No, he does not," said the woman, quietly. "Edvrai des mother has been taken ill, and he has gone down to St. Alban's to see her. You are to stop here to-night, and have his bed." "Is that, ail ?" said Samson, looking rather blank, " Yes ; only that you'll have supper with me." "Didn't Mr. Klopetock say I was to go up to his room? "No; and he isn't to be disturbed." "Has be had any row with the Woolfords 2" " No. What nonsense, man! There, go down into the kitchen. I shall he there directly." Somme Hall drooped, and went below stairs, feeling disappointed, but on finding be might emoke a pipe, and that there would be a ceuplf of glows of ale for his supper, he sealed down, and made himself com- fortable, the housekeeper going off to bed in company with the housemaid at ten o'clock, to the top of the house, and Samson Hall betaking himself to the odd man's bed downstairs in a kind of pantry, where he I was supposed to sleep for the protection of the place.

FOR the moment Mark Woolford wee so staggered by the sudden glare of light flashing upon him when he believed hico.,elf alone, that he could hardly realise the fact that a constable had been watching him from a dark entry on the other side, and had then turned on his bull's eye lanthorn. "It is all right, constalle," said Mark. "I was a little uneasy about the place, so I came and had a look round."

"Oh, was you?" said the constable, in a doubting tone. "Well, it was very good of you when there was police about. Now, then, let's have another look at you." "I am Mr. Woolford, the chief clerk here," said Mark, sharply. "But I should know your voice, policeman. Lot me see. Yes; of course. You are the officer whom we had into the manager'i room when we had that bit of trouble with the porter." " When was that ?" raid the constable, bluntly. "When was that ?" said Mark, thoughtfully. "Yes, to Ise sure. A year last April. It was at the time we had to prosecute a man about a forged cheque. You are police-constable Morrison." "Right you are, sir. I ktow you now," said the constable. " Didn't make you out at first, Mr. Wool- ford, sir; and we have to be so precious wide awake. I didn't mean to bo rude, sir."

"Oh, don't say a word about that, constable. lam very glad to find you are so upon the alert." "Alert, eh, sir? Yes, that's the word. :You've no idea of the cunning do's that are on the look out to trap us. They are ready for anything. I should have looked nice before my inspector to-morrow if your place had been robbed, and I'd let one of the parties go —took off my guard because he was so smooth and civil."
"Yes, yes, of course; you have some clever brains to fight against, con stab! e." "Indeed we have, sir; chaps as might have been Lord Mayors o' London, and Lord Chancellors, or

anything else, if they only give theirselves a screw to the right, instead of one to the wrong." "But you do catch them sometimes," said Mark, smiling. "Yes, sir: we puts the salt of the law on the tails of these little gaol-birds sometimes. Good night, sir. You needn't trouble to acme down no more to look roma here; there's one or other of us about every hour or so. Good night, sir." 'Good night, constable," said Mark; and *eV parted at the ell of the court, each going in a differ direction. They would have felt less satisfied about dieir wAchfulness if they had known that Some One 1,114. listening to what sounded like muttered words; aria soon after their footsteps had died away, the side door was softly opened and a head was thrust forth, its owner gazing up and down the court. Then he stepp?rl quickly out, closed it behind him, and walked ba.itily away. He was carrying an ordinary black leather trarel- ling-bag in one band, a rug was thrown over his arm, and he looked like some one about to start on w journey. He walked swiftly to the first cabstand, hailed S hansom, of which the driver was having a cup of coffee at a stall by the light of a flaring naphtha lamp, and, upon the man hurriedly naJunting his perch, the fare placed the bag on the footboard, leaped in, gave some hasty directions, and was driven away. Meanwhile, feeling more easy in his mind, gark Woolford walked steadily back to Brunnvick-square, reaching home in due time, quite wearied out now, and ready to sleep. As he closed the hall door, be involuntarily glanced at the hat-pegs. where a light overcoat was hanging; and on the slab lay a en° hat, and a pair of soiled white kid gloves. He noticed these gloves a good deal as he lit s chamber candlestick, and then, going softly up to bed. he saw that Martin's door was closed, and that a pair of slightly muddied patent leather shoes were We' lessly thrust outside. Martin had returned, and, judging from appearanceo, it seemed evident that he had been either to some enter tainment or to a ball. Mark stopped on the landing for a few moment°, hesitating as to whether he should speak to his brother that night. He decided that he would not, for the young man would, if awakened, be excited, the probability beil that he was plunged in a heavy slumber from which would be folly to attempt to awaken him, for if be were aroused he would be ill-used and resentful, and in ne wise ready to listen to the advice and stern admonitions of his elder brother, who had now made up his mind so to his coarse. "He must go abroad," said Mark, as he went ow 11P to his own room, little thinking, as he fell into a lie/ sleep, what stern fate was preparing against bile, an of the troubles that were to be ushered in by this coming- (To k cottiiftwa.)

The House adjrrned at twenty-five minutes to six. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

J. Eaton and Mr. Thomas Stringer. The collision at Carlisle, Light Railways in Ireland, the Postage Rates to India and the Colonies, and the conversion of the Eg,yrition Debt formed the subjects of further questions, .and Sir J. FERGIISSON informed Mr. Han- bury that no objections had been raised by the Foreign Office in reference to the Major Wissmann and Emin Pasha Expedition, seeing the assurances were spontane- ously given that the British sphere of influence would not be disturbed. Mr. Ritchie, in answer to Mr. Evans, explained that the funds placed at the disposal of County Councils for the extinction of licenses could be used for that purpose only. Mr. W. 11. Smith informed Mr. Baumann, that the Government would endeavour this 'session to bring in a Bill to amend the Factory and Workshops Act. Mr. Goschen, being asked by Mr. Storey for an explanation of his remarks at Rawtenstall, charging the Liberal party with murderous intentions towards the Allotments Bill, practically adhered to his statement. MR. GLADSTONE ON gOMPENSATION. The House went into Committee on the Budget Bill. Mr. STOREY argued that it was without precedent to im- pose a new duty before the House had decided on the policy of the purpose to which the sum raised by the new tax was to be allocated, and he moved the posponement of the clause referring to the spirit duty. Mr. GLADSTONE said it was contrary to common sense that they should be called on to vote a specific sum for a specific purpose altogether new and unknown to their previous practice without the power of discussing the merits of that pur- pose. Why should not these clauses be postponed? The subject of compensation was one of enormous weight and enormous consequence, and if the Chancellor of the Exchequer should succeed in carrying a vote of this kind in defiance of all usage and common sense, he would not find that the remaining stages ot his path on the subject would be one whit smoother or his progress more rapid. Mr. SMITH stated his willingness to postpone the con- sideration of the clauses in dispute until after the second reading of the bill appropriating the money proposed to be raised, and the clauses were postponed amid Opposi- tion cheers. Later in the evening Dr. Tanner had to be called to order for interrupting Mr. Jesse Collings. The Bill passed through Committee at five minutes past twelve o'clock. _ _ _
The Deed of Arrangement Bill passed through Com- mittee.
_ The House adjourned at 12.35 a.m

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present Allermen Holmes Burgess, Wright, and Sutton; Councillors Platt, W. Pierpoinr, Tay- lor, Cannell, Fleming, Shaw Green, Flood, Beaman, Ashton, Voisey, Jenkins, Hepherd, Tinsley, Hutch- inson, Marsh, Garner, It. T. Fairclough, Percival, Heaton, Ureenall, Bolton; Messrs. Whittle (Town Clerk), and Longdin (borough surveyor). •
THE NEW COUNCILLOR. The MAYOR reported the election of Mr. Beaman for the North-West Ward.
THE POLICE FORCE.

The minutes of the Watch Committee contained a re- port as to the borough police force by the Hon. C. G. Legge, inspector of constabulary and police forces in the northern district. The report states that during the year ending 1889, two constables resigned voluntarily, and one was called upon to do so; three were dismissed, and one was discharged with a gratuity. Thirty-four members of the force hold certificates under the St. John's Ambulance Association. The numbers and disci- pline of the force had been efficiently maintained. The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes, and this being seconded by Alderman Surros, the minutes were adopted.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended the appointment of Councillor Shaw-Green to be deputy-chairman, and of Councillor Hepherd to be a member of the Committee. Alderman HOLMES moved, and Councillor JENKINS seconded, the adoption of the minutes,which was agreed to.

NEW BUILDINGS. The Street Lnpfovement and Lighting Committee recommended approval of the plans of the following buildings :—Alterations to offices of the Warrington ,Slate Company, Limited; new shed in Napier-st., for 'Messrs. E. Forshaw and Son; five cottages in Pinner's Brow, for Dr. Fox ; five cottages and one shop in Knuts- ford-road, for Mr. John Blackburn ;alteration to property in Pinner's Brow, for Mr. Joseph Wilkinson; building line of two proposed cottages in Pinner's Brow, for Mr. Thomas Williams; six housesin Longford-st., for Mr. J. Shortland ; extension of offices in Bewsey-road, for the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Lipited. CouncillorPLArr moved the adoption of the minutes, and referred to the lose that had been sustained by the death of Mr. Greening. Councillor Melon secondeJ, and the minutes were agreed to.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE BOROUGH.-IMPORTANT DISCUSSION.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE BOROUGH.-IMPORTANT DISCUSSION.

The Sanitary Committee recommended that 335. be allowed to Mrs. Sarah McCoy as compensation for the slaughter of two pigs ordered by the Committee to be destroyed ; also the acceptance of the tender of Messrs. Joseph Gibson and Son for the erection of a manure store at Longford at £490; and that two new horses be purchased of Mr. James Warburton, of Dalian, at the price of £142 10s. with two old horses given in exchange. Councillor Beaman had been elected a member of the Committee. Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirma.ion of the minutes, said that the acceptance of the tender of Mr. Gibson was in consequence of the failure of Messrs. Catlin and Son, who had had the contract for that piece of work. Messrs. Gibson had agreed to do the work on the terms of their original tender. With regard to Mr. Beaman's appointment they thought he would be a very efficient and useful member of the Committee, and they were of opinion that he ought to take the place on the Sanitary Committee of the late Mr. Greening. Refer- ring to the purchase of the two new horses, Alderman Burgess said that in their experience they had found it better to buy good horses. Dealing with the medical officer's report, from which we gave copious extracts last week, the Aldennan said that 1,000 copies were being circulated amongst the ratepayers of the town. The report was not all the Sanitary Committee could have desired in a good many respects, the death rate for the past year being 22•12,. or 2.6 higher than 1888, and 38, the average of tht past 10 years. That was not satisfactory, and nobody would be less satisfied with it than the members ot the Sanitary Committee themselves, and it would be their duty to ascertain if they can what were the causes at work to produce these results. The same causes, or at least the same increased rate of mor- tality, had been obtaining throughout the country. So far as Warrington was concerned he was very much' at a loss ,to make it out. They would find from the report that the town had suffered considerably from brain disease —(a laugh)—they had had no• fewer than 65 deaths from the various types of brain disease. They had also had no fewer than 23 deaths from cancer. That had been a subject - of consideration with the Committee for a leagth of time. That disease seemed to be steadily growing upon them in Warrington, and he should think the increase this last year had been one-third,.. There had been no fewer than 45 cases of death from heart disease; These were all very unsatisfactory things, but he was not in a position to say that they could find out very easily the , causes or put a stop to them. (Hear, hear.) lii the I winding up of his report the medical officer said, " I hope that during the year IMO., your attention will be directed to the serious evils arising from the unhealthy areas' and unsanitary dwellings' which still exist in the Borough. This is a subject which is occupying the minds of sa,nitarians all over the• country, and f feel sure' yott will not alloy Warrington to take a secondary place." It was their bounden duty to take case,. so far as they could, that those "unhealthy areas 'r—those " Black Spots "as therwere called by some .people in Warrington—should be removed as • soon as possible. (Hear, hear.) But he was not site sure whether, while
