div.head: TIIE EXAMINER, SATITRD,VY, MAY 10, 1890
div.p: TIIE EXAMINER, SATITRD,VY, MAY 10, 1890

he a ereerl with Dr. Gornall in almost everything he did, he could quite surrender his judgment to the medical officer. Tn stigmatise a very large extent of property as being unhealthy was a very serious matter, and the harassing and worrying of owners and occupiers of pro- perry, in an unreasonable way was not at all desirable. (Hear, hear.) These things must be removed—(hear, hear)—but it must be done discreetly and with a proper attention to the necessary requirements of the case. In his opinion it was better that their medical officer of health should bring a report, every Wed- nesday if he pleased, asking for the dealing with some specified piece of property which was of the character he described in his report. He had never yet known the medical officer come with a specific charge against property that the Committee had not taken up and carried through, unless the town clerk said,the law was against them. Take, for instance, houses with no through ventilation—back to back houses. He quite agreed that these were undesirable residences for anyone to live in, but they had them in Warrington and were obliged to have them because they were in existencelbefore that authority, and the law did not allow the authority to meddle with them. While Dr. Gornall reprobated that class of property, hundreds of back to back houses were being built in one of the large towns of Yorkshire. If the Sanitary Comr,nittee could do anything towards removing nuisances affecting dwellings, whether occasioned by overcrowding, filthi- ness, or anything else, they were bound to do it. In a book that was brought before them every Wednesday they had a record of the nuisances reported by their officers and these nuisances were being steadily dealt with as they arose week by week. He thought that was the better way—bringine individual cases rather than preparing extended charges over a whole area or district. He did not want them to think that he was differing with the medical officer—it was only a question of method. In one case he might mention that their medical officer in his annual report enumerated 1,200 houses as unfit for human habitation, that was one-sixth of the whole oi the inhabited houses in the borough. But. they could not attempt to enter upon a crusade against onesixth of the inhabited houses of the borough, and they declined to accept the report, and it never was adopted. Their medical officer deserved, and should have, as far as the Sanitary Committee could give him, the utmost support in their power to carry out the work he was so anxious to have done. The work of making the streets and back passages which had been left over for a considerable period was now being vigor- ously taken in hand by the raving and Sewerage Com- mittee. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Sun.= seconded the adoption -of the minutes. Councillor SHAW GREEN mentioned that on some nights there was a most horrid stench in the neighbourhood of the Wesleyan Chapel, Bewsey-road. He had tried in various ways to ascertain whence it came hut he had not been able. It happened generally between 11 and 12 o'clock at night. Alderman BURGESS said he would take care that the matter was looked into. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH referred to the price that was being paid for the horses, and contended that really good animals could be purchased for £5O or £55 each. If they went beyond that sum they were giving a fancy price. He moved as an amendment that the minute relating to the purchase of the horses be not passed. Councillor PIERPOINT thought the price that was being given for the horses simply ridiculous, but when people bought horses for other people they could afford to give better prices than for their own. (Laughter.) The full report of their medical officer raised a great many serious matters. He referred in particular to that part which showed how many outbreaks of fever there had been in 1889 in the neighbourhood of offensive emanations from sewers. With regard to the unhealthy areas and unsanitary dwellings,he had sufficient confidence in their medical officer to believe that if he stigmatised any area as being unhealthy it was unhealthy, and he was shocked to see that they had dwellings in Warrington which were insanitary. The Sanitary Committee could not do impossibilities, but from the tone of the remarks of the chairman it seemed that the committee were anxiously looking forward to the mending of these insanitary dwellings and that at all eventswas some comfort. With regard to scarlet fever, the doctor reported that he was anxiously awaiting the completion of the map of the i borough referred to n his last year's report, to assist him in an enquiry into the reason why that disease continued to be prevalent in the borough. Dr. Gornall had asked for the map year after year, and he hoped the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee would see his way to ordering it at the earliest moment. _ _ _ . _ .

Councillor JENKINS said that 12 mrnths ago the Chair- man .f the Committee promised that the map should be completed without unnecessary delay. He also called attention to page 31 of the report, and said he regretted to find that thtrNorth-East Ward bore a most unenviable position with regard to its sanitary character. Dr. Gornall said : "This ward enjoys the unenviable privi- lege of having the highest death rate. It has the largest number of back-to-back houses, and houses with no through ventilation, and there are other dwellings where there are restrictions and impediments to the free circulation of air. This ward is also the most over- crowded, and unfortunately, remarkable for "domestic darkness" and "general dirtiness of dwellings." He (Councillor Jenkins) thought that many of the evils pointed out by the medical officer, such as unpaved pass- ages and yards, might be remedied without any delay.

Alderman SurroN said Councillor Jenkins seemed to be under the misapprehension that it was the duty of the Corporation to put the places he had referred to in order, but it was the duty of the owners of property, and if Councillor Jenkins knew the trouble the Committee had had with owners of property throughout the town he would not be making the complaints he was. They had endeavoured again and again to get these places put into sanitary condition ,but the owners had rebelled al: ainst the Committee. It would be the duty of the Corporation some day to proceed against those owners in a way that would compel them to do what was required. (Hear, hear. Councillor Fleming : That is what should be done). Alderman Sutton then defended the purchase of the horses. To give that price for a horse might not suit sonic gentlemen, but it suited the Corporation to give that amount. (Laughter.) They knew some gentlemen dicl not care to give more than 30s. apiece for horses. (Laughter.) Good horses were cheapest in the end. Councillor PIERPOINy seconded the amcndment.

Councillor noon said that he felt that the Sanitary Committee had really been unjustifiably attacked that night. His short experience of that Committee had shown him that, from the Chairman downwards, they had done their utmost to 'carry out their duties lig far as was consistent with the position that they occupied. He had known in his experience some of the strongest members of the Council to rebel against the action of the Sanitary Committee, and they had cone so

• far as to say that they considered there was personal persecution. They had charged officials with personal bias against themselves. These were among the diffi- culties that the committee had to encounter in trying to do their duty. .Parhaps he was in a positicin to speak from personal experience of the condition of a great deal of property in the borough. Since he had been elected a member of the Council,he had made it his special duty to frequently visit certain districts to which reference was made in the report of the ‘,ledical Officer, which was Itrue to the letter; no one could say that there was a line lin the report which was exaggerated., Indeed, half the truth had not been told from the fact that a medical officer was only allowed t go so far. He had made inquiries from their legal adviser., and he had been told ' that they were not empowered to expose delinquents individually and make examples of them. If they could • do so it would serve as a lesson to many persons up and down the kingdom. Ho had seen some of the most wretched hovels, which were owned by someof the most prominent citizens • but they knew that the law was weak and that the 'Corporation were not able to reach them; at least, that they could not go to the extent they would like. Owners of property to a certain extent set the Corporation at defiktice. He contended that it was the duty of the members of the Council to assist the Committee to rcot out the evils complained of. Councillor PLATT, agreed with Councillor Fairclough that £BO for a horse was too much to pay. It was use- less for any Committee to give £2O for an extra good looking horse ; nobody but a brewery company could afford to do that. • (Laughter) Councillor VOISEY defended the action of the Com- mittee in the purchase of the horses, and Councillor BYATON said he wculd not give so much for a horse for his own use ; a good one could be obtained for £BO. Councillor Bozrow contended that the members of the Corporation should at as they would if they were simply a firm. Was it wise to give -£142 10s. for two horses when animals could be hired at such a cheap rate? Re- ferring to remarks made by Councillor Flood, he con- tended that the Council Chamber should not be made a place in which to wash dirty linen ; as members of the Corporation they assembled to study the business of the , town and the interests of the ratepayers, and not to fall out whether officials did their duty straightforwardly. He had had some experience of the Committee, and in such a manner that he had not gained much credit. (Laughter). He gained no credit, because when he made a complaint it was not taken notice of. The official was not examined, but he was allowed to interro- gate him (Councillor Bolton),and did not give a satisfac- tory explanation. The MAYOR.—It is not proper for a member of the Council to discuss any matter in which he is personally interested. Councillor FLOOD rose to a point of order. He did not mention any name. The MAYOR.—No name was mentioned. Councillor BOLTON, after some further observations, said that if there was a more disgracefukthing than the open sewer that travelled through Howley, Councillor Flood would have to go further than Lancashire to find it. He need only r off Mersey-St. and look at Litton's- row, and in the neighbourhood of Rose and Crown-St., to find unsanitary property. That was property belong- ing to the Corporation. Alderman BURGESS, replying to the discussion, said that the map which had been asked for by Dr. Gornall had been photographed three or four times, but up to the present time it was a failure. No one had been able to obtain the result which Dr, Gomall required. The matter was now in the hands of a gentleman in Man- chester, but they were not hopeful that it would come out a success. It would cost a lot of money altogether, and he contended that the Committee could better afford to lay that money out in the purchase of horses rather i than n mans. If Councillor Jenkins would refer to the Medical Officer's report, he would find that the death rate for the North-East Ward was 24.78. In the North- West Ward, which, in his judgment, should be the healthiest in the town, the rate was the highest-25-27. In the South-East Ward it was 1734, in the South-West 15.75, and in Latchford 17.69. Putting the two East Wards together they had a less death rate than the aggre- gate of the West Wards. That was a rather singular fact in the face of what had been said about the depots. As to Silver-square, it was the Paving and Sewerage Committee against whom the charge should be brought by Councillor Jenkins. The best thing to be done was to summon the Committee. (Laughter.) Concerning the hire of horses, he might say that the Committee only hired them to the extent they thought desirable. It cost 50 per cent, more to hire horses than to have their own. With regard to Howley Brcs^ls, that also as a matter within the province of the Paving and Sewerage Coin. mittee. As to the remarks which had been made about certain properties off Mersey-st., Rose and Crown-st., and Bolton's-yard—(laughtsr)—he would point out that they belonged to private owners, and were not repair- able by the Corporation. He might add that the horses which had been purchased were already in the Corpora- tion stables, and the old ones had been sent d away. (Laughter.) Councillor R. Faniczonou said that, under those cir- cumstances, he would withdraw his amendment, and Councillor Pierpoint assenting to the withdrawal, the minutes were agreed to.

Public Elementary Schools during the month of February was 7,148. corresponding period last year 7,423—decrease. 275, and for the month of March, 7,573, corresponding period last year, 7,l4B—increase 425. Councillor FLEMING, in moving the adoption of the i minutes,remarked that there was one thing n the annual report which was not quite so satisfactory as could have been wished, although it had helped to reduce the cost of carrying on the good work. He referred to the item— fines £54 45. It was to be hoped that, with the improve- ment which took place in trade—but which, he was sorry to say, had vanished—that sum would be gradu- ally reduced, as the Committee had no desire to add to their income in that way. Great praise was due to Mr. Riley and his assistants for the way they had performed their arduous and, at times, not altogether pleasant duties. (Hear, hear.) They had, however, the consola- tion of knowing that the Committee appreciated their services. He was sure the Council would do so too, and that should spur the officers on to further efforts to keep up the attendance to the highest pitch, and thus prevent the town having a School Board forced upon it. (Hoar, hear.) Councillor SHAW GREEN seconded the adoption of the minutes, observing that the difficulties of the Committee were largely brought about by the action of school- masters in sending children home because they happened to go to school without their pence. The names were then returned to the Committee as "absentees." A little more leniency on the part of the masters was desirable. There were a great many people who objected to a School Board for Warrington, and it would be a pleasure to them to know that at present the schools in the town furnished ample accommodation for the children.

The minutes were passed. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The return for the month of March showed that the number of visitors to the Museum was 3,898, a decrease of 15 pier cent. compared with March. 1889; books issued in reading-room 1,783, decrease 2 per cent.; lending de- partment 2,558. increase 2 per cent. The following gifts had been made to the Museum :—" The Naturalist,' 1889, arepidoptera,93 specimens, Plants, mounted for the Herbarium, 37 sheets from the Field Club; nest and eggs of Greenfinch, old tobacco pipe, from the Town Clerk; "Antiquarian's spade and pencil," by Ward, from Mr. W. H. Woodcock; pair of clogs, from Mr. William DFbl- shire. Councillor Monks had been appointed senior vice- chairman, and Councillor H. Roberts junior vice-chair- man of the Committee. The minutes of the Committee were adopted on the motion of Alderman SurroN, seconded by Councillor SHAW GREEN.

CEMETERY COMMITTEE. From the report of the registrar to the Cemetery Com- mittee it appeared that the interments for the past six weeks were :—Adults, 34; minors, 111; stillborn and premature, 20. And for the corresponding period last year :—Adults, 49; minors, 52; stillborn and prema- ture, 15. The receipts for the At six weeks were £139 Bs. 9d., awl for the corresponding period last year £9B 13s. 9d. The Committee recommended acceptance of the tender of Mr. Henry Hoult for the painting, &c., required at the cemetery at £52. The minutes were adopted on the proposition of Coml. cillor TAYLOR, seeollded by GbuncillOr ASIITON.
THE TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COHHITTIRE.-THE

div.head: NEW STREETS.
div.p: NEW STREETS.

The Paving and Sewerage Committee's minutes con- tained the following resolution :—That the tender of Mr. Thomas Allen for the labour required in forming and paving the following streets be accepted, viz. :—Ellis-st. at £l4 9s. 7d., Hoyle-st. at £75 18s. 6d. David-st. at £l5 13s. 6d.; that the tenders of Mr. William Williams for the labour required in forming and paving of the following streets be accepted :—Helsby-st at £32 4s. Bd., Stephen-st. at £7 183. 4d., Atherton-st. at £9 10s. 11d., Back Atherton-st. at £3 14s. 6d. ; that the tenders of Mr. Simeon Hough for the labour required in forming and paving of the following streets be accepted :—Brack- lev-st. £22 25. 81., Garibaldi-st. £24 is., Baxter-st. £l2 95. 2d. The tender of Mr. William Taylor to supply 12 concrete mixing boards at £7 had been accepted. Alderman WRIGHT, in moving the adoption of the report of this Committee, said that the Committee were pushing on with street-makint, as fast as they were able, it being their desire to help the Sanitary Committee to the ' best of their powers. With reference to Howley Brook, a mutter which might seem to be progressing but slowly, the Committee were obliged to move in it very cauti- ously. There were a great many interests which had to be considered, and a number of people had to be dealt with before they could go to work in a legal and proper manner. As soon, however, as the Committee could deal with the matter effectively they would do so. Councillor HurciiiNsON seconded the motion, and the minutes were adopted.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE,
The report of the Inspector to the School Attendance Committee showed that the average attendance at the

div.head: VOLUNTEER LEASE.
div.p: VOLUNTEER LEASE.

The report of the bath-keeper showed that the income from the baths during the past week was £6 ss. 2d., and for the corresponding period last year 15s. The Committee recommended that the following members be appointed members of the Baths Sub-Committee :—The Mayor. Councillors Bolton (convener), Cannel!, Heaton, Muir ; that the following members be appointed mem- bers of the Gardens Sub-Committee, viz :—Mr. Alderman Harrison, Mr. Councillors Bolton, n d Muir. The following letter had been received by the Town Clerk from Messrs. Buckton, Greenall and Buckton, on behalf of the Volunteers :—" We have received your letter of the 6th instant, informing us that the Corpora- tion will renew the lease of the Drill Hall, &c., for a further term of three years. As the Finance Committee of the Corps will have to consider, in a few days, the advisability of erecting additional buildings on the land in question, we shall be obliged by your informing us whether the Corporation agree that the Corps may at any time remove any buildings which they may erect in the future term as well as those which are already erected." —ln regard to this letter the Committee passed the following resolution :—" That the Corps be allowed to remove any new buildings erected during the further term of three years upon an undertaking to make good all damage, and to leave the premises in a condition satisfactory to the Corporation at the termination of the teliancy.n Councillor Heaton had been\ appoint 4 member of the gardens sub-comrnltte. The Comlnittee recommended that the tender of Mr. William Winstanley to re-cover the back steps in the Town Hall with lead, at £4 10s., with an allowance of 12s. per cwt. for the old lead, be accepted. The MAYOR proposed, and Councillor BOLTON seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor FLOOD remarked that he found no provision had been made for the better accommodation of bands in the park. It would be well to take the matter in hand, as it was for the benefit of the public. (Hear, hear.) Another entrance to the park was also needed. The im- provement at the far end, the widening of the Kendrick- street gateway, had been much appreciated, and an en- trance from Crosfield-street w)uld be equally appre- ciated. _ _ _

Councillor PLArr quite agreed with Councillor Flood as to the necessity for proper accommodation for the bands—(hear, hear)—because he thought that the bands playing in the park were a great attraction to the public, and the matter was therefore well worthy of the sup- port and countenance of the Corporation. As to an en- trance from Crosfield-street, he saw no necessity for it. (Hear, hear.) It would only accommodate the few people who lived in Crosfield-street • moreover, it would leave the park more open to the depredations of outsiders and children. Alderman Sorrox said the Committee had had the question of a band stand under their consideration on many occasions, and they were of opinion that as £BO had been paid for the present bandstand they could not very well give it up without some attempt to make it convenient and suitable for the purpose for which it was required. He believed the present stand could be con- verted into such a band stand as everybody wanted. With regard to the additional entrance, he had always been opposed to that, on the ground that the more en- trances there were the greater the difficulty would be experienced in keeping out rough people. The minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: MARKETb.
div.p: THE MARKETb.

The Markets Committee recommended that the ten- der of Mr. John Chorley, for a small portable forge at £3 125. 6d., be accepted ; also, that a sand blast appara- tus be purchased for use in stamping glass measures.

The total income of the Committee from all sources dur- ing the past four weeks was .£342 9s. 10d. Confirmed on the proposition of Councillor GusaNALL, seconded by Councillortoresussox. GAS. COMMITTER. This Committe recommended that Councillor Hepherd be a member in place of the late Councillor Greening. The average illuminating power of the gas during the past four weeks was reported as equal to 18.6 candles, at both works. Alderman Howass proposed, and Alderman WRIGHT seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor MUIR wished to remind the Chairman of the Gas Committee that two or three months ago, when we had a little bit of a stir about the illuminating quality of the gas, it suddenly ruse to something respectable. It was then 188 candles. Since that time it had reached 18.36 candles. That was very respectable; but this last month it had, unfortunately, descended to 18-6 candles. He hoped the Chairman of the Committee would look after that for the benefit of the burgesses. Alderman HOLMES : Councillor Muir seems to have fallen into a very simple error. He has forgotten his schooldays. He says that the average illuminating power was 18.36 and is now 18.6 candles. It is quite clear that the candles of 18.6 are of a better value than 1836. (Laughter.) Tilt; Maxon : It is the decimals that are bothering Councillor Muir. (Loud Laughter.) The minutes were agreed to. THE WATERWORKS PIIRCHASE.—CORPORATION OFFICIAL'S

EXPENSES. The following resolutions were in the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, viz :—That the Town Clerk be instructed te take such steps as he may consider necessary for the promotion of the Improvement Bill: that the Mayor and Aldermen Burges, Harrison, and Sutton, be re-aopointed a Sub-Committee to wait upon the directors of the Water Works Company on the sub- ' ject of the proposed purchase of the Water Works under- taking, particularly with regard to an examination of the company's property and accounts, and report thereon to this Committee; that the Borough Surveyor be in- structed to obtain the report of a geologist on the per- manency of the supply of water Of the Warrington Water Works undertaking: that the Town Clerk write to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, withdrawing the notice served upon the company on the Ist February, 1888, requiring the construction of a bridge in the deviation railway of the Warrington and Stock- port line of the London and North-Western Railway; that the follo,wing officials be allowed when out of town on corporation business, first class railway fare and cab fares, and if unavoidably detained all night, the sum of £lls. per day, and when not so detained the sum of 10s. 6d. per aay, namely :—The Borough Treasurer, Borough Surveyor, and Medical Officer of Health; that Mr. Councillor Pierooint be appointed a member of the Parliamentary Sub-Committee; that the Rev. M. Rigby, ' of St. Peter's, be allowed the use of the buildine in John- st., belonging to the Corporation, at an annual rent pi 55., subject to three months' notice, and on the condllion that the building be not used for religious servicee„ The minutes were adopted on the motion a ie Mayor, seconclEA by 4.14.r!T1F1 s.l7rNi and OA Council then rose.

div.head: COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

No fewer than 34 members of tho Opposition have given notice to move the rejection of the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Duties Bill, among them being Mr. Caine, Sir W. Lawson, Mr. Burt, Mr. P. Stanhope, and Mr. R. T. Reid. _ _ _

Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., has reprinted, with the title of " No compensation to Publicans," the two letters he wrote in 1888 on the amount of the com- pensation payable under the Government proposals both in the country districts and in the mercopoli- tan area. These two letters contain importatit data showing that the result of the plan then brought forward by Mr. Ritchie and now revived would be to "endow the liquor trade at from £200,000,000 to £250,000,000, the great bulk of which will go Woe the pockets of monopolist brewers and distillers, and not into those of the tenants of public-houses." In re-issuing these facts Mr. Caine says that" to confer a large vested interest, declared by law to be non-existent, which can only be extinguished by enormous money payments out of the taxes or rates, will place the - whole temperance movement at such hopeless disadvantage in its struggle against intemperance that no compensation pro- posal § VIM to be even entertained by Parliament apart gni the geneffil measure dealing with the entire subject of licensing legislation." LOCAL PROTESTS.

On Tuesday evening there ;;;;;a meeting at the Mis- sion Room, Latchford, of the Bonehill branch lodge of Good Templars. Mr. F. Jenkins occupied the chair, and gave a suitable address. On the motion of Brother A. Dutton, seconded by Brother J. Ellison, it was unani- mously resolved : That the proposal in the Budget to give the County Councils £350,000as a fund trom which to compensate publicans whose license for One year and no longer may not be granted, is a dangerous innovation in the direction of establishing a vested interest in liquor licenses, and this meeting therefore protests against the obnoxious scheme, and respectfully asks the Government to withdraw it ; and failing such abandonment, requests members of Parliament to vote against it." On Tuesday evening also there was a meeting of Good Templars at Lymm, which was presided over by Mr. Luke Ellison, of Latcliford, and a resolution similar in terms to the above was adopted on the motion of Brother R. Dutton, seconded by Sister Gorton.
MAY QUEEN FESTIVITIES AT GOLBORNE,

The annual festivities in celebration of the advent of May took place at Golborne, on Saturday afternoon, and were a great success. This was in a great measure due to the beautiful summer-like weather with which the gathering was favoured, but a great deal of credit was reflected upon the committee of management, for their admirablearrangementsand the commendable manner in which they were carried out. The committee consisted of Messrs. E. Last (chairman), J. Unsworth, T. Mort, J. Bate, J. Wakefield, senior, J. Wakefield, junior, J. Pim- blett, W. Battersby, J. Clayton, J. Byrom, P. Cook, Jas. Halsall, Alfred Caunce (treasurer), and Joseph Sankey, (secretary.) Visitors from the surrounding country districts began to arrive at Golbome in the forenoon and early in the afternoon the streets had an animated appearance. During the day some thousands cf spec- tators thronged the streets. The " headquarters ' of the festivities were centred in the Recreation ground, and here there were many attractions. The centre of the grounds was reserved for the May Queen demonstrators, while the borth re were occupied by swing boats, shows, hobby horses, nut and gingerbread stalls, and all the usual accompaniments of a fair. A practical commencement of the "rejoicings" was made about two o'clock, when the children who were to par- ticipate in the proceedings, began to assemble on the field. Here they were placed in their respective divisions for the grand procession. The whole of the marshalling arrangements were carried out under the orders of Dr. Dobb, whose official post was that of master of ceremon- ies. A start was made from the grounds shortly before three o'clock, and the route of the procession was crowded with spectators. The Golborne brass band, un- der the conductorship of Mr. Cook, was at the head, and they were followed by over 1,000 children representing different nations, trades, and characters. First Came flower girls, who were followed by the butchers, hospital nurses, the Gipsy Queen and her tribe, bakers, weavers, soldiers, gleaners. sailors, Red Riding Hoods, footballers, a lurry with Little 80-Peep and Boy Blue, colliers, and the Ashton Brass Band, under the leadership of Mr. Higson. Next came the Swiss peasant dancers, who were succeeded by a company of Colonel Thomp- son's Manchester miniature volunteers, who formed a guard of honour to the May Queen. The little "men." who were attired in true military uniform, with car- bines and other arms complete, attended as a guard of honour to Prince Albert Victor on the occasion of his visit to Manchester. The May Queen was preceded by- the sceptre bearer (Mr.?. Russell), and the crown hearer (Mr. P. Skelhorn). Het Majesty was Miss Annie Wake- field, twelve years of age, daughter of Mr. John Wake- field, of High-st., and she secured the royal post as a re- sult of the ballot, among the many youthful aspirants. She was dressed in a pret'y pale blue plush, trimmed with silk, and other decorations, and rode in a carriage drawn by four greys. She carried a handsome bouquet of flowers, and was attended by postillions, pages (Mas- ters John Evans and E. Walker), beefeaters (Masters Peter Wright and Wm. Hill). Next came a carriage con- taining the ex-Queen (Miss Emily Mitchell), with her maids of honour. The order of the remaining por- tion,of the procession was as follows t—Blacksmiths, strikers. milkmaids, 'Britannia" (Mi.s Ellen Cook), attended by ".England" (Miss B Walker), " Ire- land", (Master Samuel Higgins), "Scotland" (Miss S. A. Davies, and "Wales" (Miss Annie Naylor). "Darby" and "Joan" were the next characters, and they were followed by "old men" and "old women," hat-binders, stone masons, the seasons, Old Mother Hubbard, plasterers, slaters. shoemakers, doggers, the " U'po Bo troupe of dancers," the Firs-lane brass band, and the May Pole dancers. The route of the procession was along Grundv-st., up Legh-st.. Peter-st., Heath-st., Church-st., to the Smithies, returning by vrav of Bridge-of.. and Ca unce's- court. On the return to the field SOMP May Pole dancing preceded the interesting feature of the afternoon—the coronation of the May Queen. This was gracefully per- formed on an attractive "throne" of red, blue, and white cloth, decorated with national banners. The ex- queen placed the crown on thy head of her Majesty amid cheers and she handed to the Queen a purse containing one guinea as a memento of her occupation of the royal post. The three bands then played the National Anthem. Col. Thompson's minatnre volunteers went through a series of smart exercises, the " U'po Bo" troupe of dancers gave one of their grotesque performaneei ' • and dances by the Swiss peasants, and the principal charac- ters, &e., followed. The hands afterwards played for general dancing until dusk.

FUNERAL OF AIR. EDWIN WA UGH.

The mortal remains of the late Mr. Edwin Waugh were removed on Saturday from New Brighton to Manchester. for interment in St. Paul's churchyard, Kersal Moor. At half-past eleven the coffin containing the body of the lamented Lancashire Rod was taken from his residence, The !lollies, in the pregnce of Messrs. B. Liddle, A. Tweedale, G. Thompson, and T. Moorhouse, who accompanied the remains of their late friend to Man- chester. where a large number of relatives, friends, and admirers awaited their arrival. The body was enclosed in a lead shell, which was covered by a massive pan- nelled oak coffin with brass mountings, the nameplate bearing the following inscription :—" Edwin Waugh, born 29th January, 1817 ; died 30th April, 1890." An open hearse had been supplied by Messrs. Kendal, Milne, and Co.,undertakers' Manchester, and in this the body was conveyed by road to Seacombe, and thence on the luggage-boat to Liverpool, where a special carriage on the two o'clock express from Lime-street had been provided. It was arranged that the procession should leave Exchange Station, Manchester, immediately after the arrival gf the express, in order to reach Kersal Moor at half-past three. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev. Canon Crane, of the Manchester Cathdial and the Rev. Prebendary MacDonald, rector of Kersal Moor, and a full choral service was performed by the surplice(' choir from the cathedral. Some thousands of people gathered along the way from the railway station to Kersal, a distance of two miles and a half, and tl • church and grounds were crowded. The grave, whi(h had been decorated with flowers and foliage, is in fill view of the Moor, which was a favourite place with Mr. Waugh. To each person in the church was handed a leaflet, on which were set down the words. " In memray of Edwin Waugh; born January 29, 1817 ; died Apr I. 30, 1890."

div.p: Several letters are again crowded out.

Dynamite is now being used for felling trees, Boma experiments by military authorities at Copenhagen having proved very successful. There seems to be plenty of " progress " with the forces pf destruction; what is wanted is more progress in construction.

Lord Randolph Churchill's private secretary has informed a correspondent that his lordship is not a total abstainer, nor has he joined any temperance league." Very good; but, as he is interesting him- iii the cause of temperance, it may at least be said that he is a member of the Band of Hope.

-- The Court of Appeal has just decided that the general Council of the Education and Registration Qf the United Kingdom were justified in striking eff the register of dental surgeons a dentist named Partridge, who sought business by advertising. This is Trade Unionism with a vengeance I And it is hard on newspapers, too,—this prohibition egaiust advertising.

Mr. Chaplin has intimated that, as rabies is greatly on the decline, he hopes to be in a position, at no very distant date, to suspend the muzzling _o_rder, or substitute a registration order for it. but why not extend the muzzling order to every ,ounty in England, if it is doing good work, and ~keen it up" until hydrophobia is entirely svern ped out? Better not have begun than leave e job half done. th

The Liberal Unionists are in anything but a 11412Py frame of mind as to the Tithes Bill. They don't like it, as it stands, and yet they are afraid of going against the Government. There was a Meeting on the subject on Tuesday ; and Lord llartington' who presided, sought to drill them into order ;13tit they are an awkward squad as yet, aid it is understood that they will have to be sub- jected to another drill.

There is some prospect of a debate between Mr. Bradtlaugh and Mr. John Burns on the eight hours' question, the member for Northampton being oPposed to legislative compulsion. It will be a grand encounter; but it is hardly to be expected that the Socialist leader will prove equal to Mr. Brad- laugh, who has had training on a hundred plat- forms.
Stanley is the hero of the hour, and he is being feasted and flattered by everybody, from the Queen

downwards. He and his brave comrades are certainly entitled to all the square meals they can get, either for love Or money, considering the way they had to starve in "Darkest Africa." The story of their journey through hundreds of miles of dense forest has no equal in either ancient or modern history.

The Edinburgh Town Council, at a meeting held on Tuesday, resolved to confer the freedom of the city on Mr. H. M. Stanley, "as he first came into fame in connection with the explorations of a great Scotchman, Dr. Livingstone." Let Welshmen beware; they have claimed Stanley as a country- man; but if he once gets to the Northern capital they will make him out to be a Scotchman.

" Scribner's Magazine " for Juno will occupy the unique position of being alone in the field with an important illustrated article from the pen of the great explorer. It is a matter of course to say that there will be a great run on the number. Stanley's book will soon follow, 'and it is to be fol- lowed in its turn by an article entitled—" How Stanley wrote his book." If the public take to this sort of snobbery, we may expect the article to be succeeded by an article describing how the article was written.

Sir Frederick Leighton called attention, at the Academy banquet, on Saturday, to the fact that England is behind France and Germany in the matter of a Gallery Of National Art. There is plenty of material, but it wants bringing together under one roof. We have what is called the National Gallery, in Trafalgar Square, and there is the South Kensington Collection. There is, too, a permanent exhibition at Dulwich—not much fre- quented by visitors, though it is well worth a visit. A unity of this trinity would make a really splen- did collection.

It is a sign of the times when the Government narrowly escape defeat on a land question. In the House of Commons, on Tuesday evening, Mr. R. 1 T. Reid introduced a motion to the effect that al measure was urgently needed enabling town councils and county councils in England to acquire by agreement, or compulsion, such land within and adjoining their districts as might be needed for the requirements of the inhabitants On being put to the vote, the motion was defeated by 16 votes only. It is the Tory doctrine, it must be remembered, that the land is for the "upper ten," and not for the people. • The authorities of New South Wales are in des- pair. Two years ago, they offered a reward of £25,000 for any method or process that would result in the extermination of that pest of the colony—the rabbit—but the reward is as yet un- earned. It is a pity Australia is so far away. If all the hungry East-enders could be turned once a week amongst the rabbits they would soon make short work of them. There is an old saying that "God never sends mouths without sending meat"; but when mouths and meat are 10,000 miles apart it is a little awkward.

As they say in the "Mikado "—" Here's a how- d'ye-'do ! Here's a pretty mess!" There is a per- son in Melbourne k.lown as the Rev. Nathaniel Kinsmar who has married as many as 7,000 couples. This is bk..d enough or good enough—just as the reader may take it—but the mischief is, that it has lately been discovered that the cham- pion. knot-tyer is a seceder from the Anglican Church and has never been ordained! It is for the lawyers now to say whether his knots are all slip-knots; and there is, whilst the point is under consideration' no small agitation in 14,000 bosoms. There are, to be sure, one or two couples who are agreeably excited at the prospect of a happy re- lease.

It is well-known that the late Richard Cobden took a great interest in the land question' and the preservation of commons. It is stated on the authority of his daughtQr that the last words he ever spoke were : " Tis a great sin for man or woman To steal a goose from off a common, But who would plead that man's excuse Who steals thP common from the goose?" There are various renderings of this epigram, and the best we have seen runs as follows : We put in goal the man or woman Who steals the goose from off the common; But leave the greater felon-loose Who steals the common from the goose

The fifth report of the " Sweating" Commis- sion was issued on Monday. It is an interesting, but pathetic document. It makes one think that rather than exist in this civilised and Christian country, under some of the Bonditions set forth, it we re better to dwell with Stanley's pigmies in the forest primeval. It is admitted that the poor do their duty to each other; and yet,—well, there is blame somewhere. The Commissioners recom- mend "immediate Parliamentary interference; " but they might just as well recommend a trip to the moon. Immediate interference, forsooth, when Parliament cannot get through a tithe of its work! When shall we have the sense to establish four Home Rule Parliaments; and over- take some of our arrears? ' ,

, - The "sweated," poor wretches, must continue to toil on and die off in the unhealthylmiserable sties which do duty as workshops; the men at their wits' end every week to keep body and soul to- gether, and the women in many cases eking out their starvatiop wages "on the streets." And all the while in this " Merrie England" of ours (" inerrie " indeed!) no less than one hundred millions of money are year by year added to the wealth of the nation. Why cannot a fair share of this wealth go to these down-trodden toilers P That is a question which these starvlinas will answer ere long by blows and blood, if they can get no other answer; and they will be justified in" strik- ing" for a chance of "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness."

Last week the Daresbnry Highway Board unani- mously decided not to accept a high level vehicular bridge across the Ship Canal, if the swing bridge at Ackers-lane had to be sacrificed. In taking this course, they were acting in harmony with the recommendations of their own Sub-Committee and with the expressed w:shes of the inhabitants of Latchford. On Thursday last, however, the question was again before the Board; and—wonderful to state —the Board decided to stultify itself by rescinding its previous resolution,and accepting the high level vehicular bridge. But the latest decision is obvi- ously illegal, for a resolution once carried cannot be rescinded except upon due notice of a motion to that effect to every member of the Board. This point should be raised; and, beyond that, it iS due to the residents of Latchford to take their opinion upon this sudden and mysterious nver6al of policy. It means that two swing bridges—ono at Grappenhall-road,and another at Acker's-lane—are to be sacrificed for one high-level bridge.

A RAOE STAKEHOLDER SUED. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Mr. J. Goldthorpe, of Manchester, who sat as deputy in the absence of Judge Shand, heard a case in which Frederick Gaiter a collier, living at Haydock, claimed £2:5 from Mr. Edward littlton, proprietor of the Sporting Chionicle," Manchester, and Robert Shaw, a collier living at Downsll Green, the amount of the stakes deposited with the "Sporting Chronicle," in a footrace between Gaiter and Shaw, which took place at the Star Inn Race Grounds, St. Helens; on the 22nd February last. Mr. 11. L. Riley appeared for plaintiff; ',Mr. Sparrow, barrister instructed by Messrs. Cobbett and Co., Manchester) represented Itir4Hulton.and Shaw defended in person. Mr. Sparrow stated that the race was run and the referee (Mr. Gorton, from the "Sporting Chronicle" tiffice) gave it in favour of Shaw. Gaiter said it was not fair, and he wanted the money. Shaw said :" I won the race, and the stakes belong to me," and the case had been brought before his hon- our to decide between the men. The money was waiting for the decision of the court, and Mr. 'W- WII did not care to which man the money had to be paid. It had been waiting for decision for two months, and had actually been paid into court pend- ing such decision. Mr. Riley then made a statement for for the original plaintiff.—His Honour said Mr. Sparrow had no doubt taken a safe course for Mr. Hutton in leaving the matter to the court, but he could not see that any one else was entitled to the £25 which Gaiter had deposited than Gaiter him- self, and he gave judgment for him.

another question, for the gradient is somewhat stiff, and that means more wear and tear, and more dan- ger of horses being down. The tradesmen of Bridge Street are strongly of opinion, however, that wood Paving would suit them ; and they are taking steps to bring their views before the Town Council. The top end of Bridge Street is absurdly narrow it is like the neck of a bottle as compared with the lower end—and, with a steadily increasing traffic, we can well understand the Shopkeepers' cry for "Peace, peace, when there is no peace." They are not unaware of the advantage which a few of their brethren have secured in Sankey Street, and they are naturally anxious to have a share of such good things in the way of pavement as are to be had. Unless it can be shown that it would be altogether too danger- ous to try what can be done in Bridge Street, it Seems to us that respect should be paid to the Wishes of an important body of tradesmen, and that an experiment in wood paving should be made. It might be tried in the first instance Where the gradient is least unfavourable, an exten- sion following on the line of safety. Wood setts have been laid down in many towns and cities since the question Was last under consideration by the Corporation of Warrington, and there should be no difficulty in ascertaining whether, and to What extent, it has answered with gradients similar o that of Bridge Street. It should be borne in mind, that it is not alone a tradesman's question. life will be more tolerable to the inhabitants at large, when there is less to be heard of the din of the streets.

SOME discussion on the annual More About "Black Spots." report of the Medical Officer of Health took place on Tuesday, at a meeting of the Warrington Town Council; and it would be well for the town if the questions raised were further considered. Referring first to a minor point, we cannot but regard it as a reflec- tion upon the Sanitary Committee that their chief Officer should have to ask year after year for a Suitable map of the borough. such a map as Dr, GonisTALL requires could, ye believe, be prepared and issued in a few weeks; and it is a very poor Joke on the part of the Chairman of the Committe e to say they could better afford to spend money on horses than maps. As much ought to have been saved out of the £l6O spent on the two horses as Would have supplied the whole town with maps. With regard to that portion of the report which deals with the "Black Spots" of Warrington, Alderman BURGESS said he could not surrender his Judgment to that of the Medical Officer of Health. But what of that? The question is—Are the statements correct? Dr. GORNALL speaks of that which he knows, and testifies of that which he has seen ; and he is confirmed, if confirmation is needed, by the special articles which have appeared in this journal, and by Councillor noon, who said "he had made it his special duty to frequently visit certain districts to which reference had been made in the Report of the Medical Officer, which Was true to the letter; no one could say that there was a line in the R3port which was exaggerated." There is another member of the Sanitary Com- mittee who has visited these "Black Spots," and he is emphatic in affirming that he had no idea that there was anything so bad in War- rington. Let Alderman BURGESS take the trouble to make a similar round of inspection before going out of his way to minimise the statements of the Medical Officer of Health. But the Chair- man of the Sanitary Committee himself practically admits,that there is something seriously wrong. "In North-West Ward," he says, "which should be the healthiest ward in the town, the death- rate was the highest-25'27." Surely, if this be the case, it is a matter calling for immediate in- vestigation. It is appalling to think that the mor- tality of the largest ward of the town is fifty per cent higher than that of the two smallest wards, namely, South West and Latchford. If Alder- man BURGESS is right in saying North-West Ward should be the healthiest ward in the town, he ought to leave no stone unturned, as Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, until he has ascertained, and if possible stopped, the cause or causes of this awful sacrifice of life. It is suggestive that the mortality of North-East Ward, Which is next in size to North-West Ward, is no less than 24.75. Putting the two north wards together, which have been alike singled out by us and by the Medical Officer of Health as distin- guished for ".Black Spots," we find that the morta- lity is 25 per thousand, whilst the average of the Other three wards is 17 per thousand. In other words the death-rate of the" Black Spots" portion Of the borough is, broadly speaking, 50 per cent. higher than that of the rest of the town. We repeat—the facts are appalling, and call for further and immediate investigation.

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The Rev. J. Simpson M.A., formerly of Stockport, commenced his pastorate of this chap(.l on Sunday, when he preached two sermons to large congregations.

Sr. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CRIMEA, Rusnitx. The Rev. J. Pulford Villiani, of BAlallege, who is 'expected to take cliarge of this chapel in August, preached the anniversary vrawns on Sunday to good congrega- tions,

POOR, RATE VOII STOCKHAM. At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magis- trates sanctioned the levying of a poor rate of Is. 2d. in the for the town:hip of Stoukham. The rate is A estimated to realise £5O Sc. 9d. 'RUNCORN SCARE BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY. An appropriation in connection with each of the two Runcorn Societies was held on Thursday evening. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. In connection with this society a tea party and enter- tainment were given on Monday evening. The young people went through a miscellaneous programme in good style. In the course of the evening Mrs. Preston dis- tributed medals, the gift of the curate, Mr. Saunderson, to those boys and girls who had been most regular in their attendance. Sr. BEDE'S SCHOOL, APPLETON.

Messrs. Sayce and Randle,contractors, have commenced the erection of a new wing to St. Bede's Catholic School. The new portion will be 42 feet long by 35 feet wide, and will contain a large class-room for girls, and a similar room for infants, together with a gallery for the latter. It is estimated that there will be extra accommodation for 200 scholars. The cost is put down at £5OO.

WIDNES BICYCLE CLUB. A club has been formed under the above title, and already possess a membership of 20 members. The pre- sident is Mr. N. Wade Deacon, J.P. ; vice-president, Captain Lewis ; secretary, Mr. C. Owen; treasurer, Mr. T. Jones; captain, Mr. W. G. Bucknall ; sub-captain, Mr. F. Sherratt ; bugler, Mr. T. Coupe. A series ofi runs to pleasant localities in Lancashire and Cheshire have been arranged.

FOUND DROWNED AT WIDNES. On Thursday evening the body of a man, unknown, was taken from the Mersey at Widnes, and now lies at the Mersey Hotel, awaiting identification. The body, which does not appear to have been long in the water, is apparently that of a man about 35 or 40 years of age. He is of fresh complexion, with dark hair, moustache, and slight imperial. His clothing consists of a black cardigan jacket, dark grey tweed vest, cord trousers,long grey stockings, low shoes with grey cloth tops, cotton shirt, and blue and white silk necktie.

ALLEGED ROBBERY AT RUNCORN. At Runecrn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Ann Regan was charged with stealing a dress from a clothes line, the property of Jane Boden. The parties are neighbours and live at Mersey View, Halton-rd. It was alleged thap Mrs. Roden placed the dress on the clothes line about eight o'clock on Saturday night, and two hours later she missed it. Subsequently she went into the prisoner's house and saw the dress in a tub. The dress was event- ually ,recovered from an outbuilding. The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and the Bench did not consider the case proved and discharged her.

FALSE PRET'ENCES AT RUNCORN. Yesterday, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. G. L. Wigg, Thomas Gallagher, a labourer, on the Ship Canal Works, was charged with having, in February, obtained by false pretences a quan- tity of wearing apparel from Ann Ingram, of Lea-ane. The prisoner went to the house of the prosecutrix and stated that her husband, who worked at Ice, had sent him for his clothes, and on that representation they were handed to him. It was afterwards ascertained that there was no truth in this statement, and that the Prisoner had run away with the clothes. He was appre- hended on Wednesday: and was now committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. BENEFIT CONCERT AT WESTON POINT. A large audience assembled on Monday evening, at the Church Schoolroom, Weston Point, when a concert Was held for the benefit of Mr. W. Thornton, who met with an accident on the Ship Canal works about three months ago. The chair was taken by Mr. H. .F. Gooch, M.E., and a well selected programme was gone through, con- sisting of songs, piccolo and cornet solos, the persons taking part being Messrs. D. Lymm, J. White, E. Yar- wood, F. Skipper, J. Bibby, T. Nicholl, W. Ferguson, H. Bann, A. Stringer, R. Thomas, and S. Collinge. The concert was thoroughly enjoyed, and Mr. W. Grounds presided at the pianoforte with his accustomed ability. LICENSING MATTERS AT RUNCORN. The Runcorn magistrates on Monday granted the transfer of the following licenses :—The Weaver Hotel, ' Weston Point, from the late Mrs. Clark to Joseph White- head Clark, her son; The Queen's Hotel, Waterloo-road, from John McCamma,ck, to Thomas Whitfield; The Ship Inn, Heath-road, front Sane Griffiths to Robert Beckett; The Royal Oak beerhouse, St. John-st., from Mary bode to Arthur Crowther. Mr. Wm. Hughes, occupier of the confectioner's shop lately occupied by Miss Alice Parsons, applied for the transfer of the license to sell wines and this was granted. John Tort was granted temporary authority to sell at the Village Inn, formerly occupied by Charles Whitfield. SKOCKING FATALITY AT WIDNES. yfenry Morgan, a man about sixty years of age, em- ployed to do "odd jobs" by Mr. Thonias Radley, of the Commercial Hotel, Old Marsh, Widnes, met with a shocking death oh Thursday. For the purpose of white- washing the rear wall Of the house, Morgan con- structed a scaffiofd of two planks, and in spite of the caution of Mr. Radley against using such a structure, he got upon the planks and commenced to work. Shortly afterwards a man named Dawson heard a bucket fall, and proceeding to the spot found Morgan on the flags. He was bleeding from the mouth and a wound on the head, his skull was fractured, his wrist broken, and one leg was injured. He died in a few minutes. AN UNGRATEFUL SAILOR AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday,Thomas Davy, a sailor, 18 years of age, was brought up on remand charged with stealing a quantity of wearing apparel, worth 305., the property of Henry Forster, a hand on board the schooner Bessie. On the night of the 21st April, the prisoner asked the men on the Bessie if they would allow him to sleeo in the forecastle, as he was locked out of his lalgings. He was given permission, and next morning, when Foster awoke at 7 o'clock, he dis- covered that the prisoner had decamped and taken the apparel with him. He was apprehended on the same day as he was about to leave the port on the steamship Tully Gorum, and he was wearing some of the stolen clothing at the time. Superintendent Large said the prisoner had made several false statements to the police, and although they had distributed his photograph throughout the country, they had been unable to trace him. The 'prisoner, who conducted himself in a very defiant fashion in the dock, was sentenced to three months' hard labour. Ural: WINALLIE CYCLE CO.'S patents can be smiled to existing machines.—Adrt.

A VIOLENT LUNATIC AT WIDNES. • A respectably dressed man named Robert Edward Eady, was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Siturday, charged with being a wandering , lunatic. Two constables were placed in the dock with him and he was also handcuffed. About seven o'clock on thcprevions evening, P.C. Davy, saw the prisoner acting in a curious manner in Lowerhouse-lane, and in consequence brought him to the police station. When placed in a cell, he be- haved in a most violent fashion and threeconstables had to beplaced in charged of him to prevent him injuring himself. Whilst the constable was giving evidence in court, the prisoner frequently shouted excitedly" It's a lie ; its all false." During a rational interval the prisoner stated that he was a clerk and shoemaker at Northamp- ton, and he did not know how he ot to Widnes. The magistrates ordered the prisoner to be handed over to the relieving officer. THE OLD LOWTON .MILL. The mean' temperature of the month was 43'48 F., nearly half a degree colder than the average tem- perature of the corresponding month of the pre- vious four years The highest temperature recorded was 66, and on the last day of the month, higher than any recorded in the same month in 1887-8-9, but exceeaed by four degrees in 1886, when it reached 70 F. The lowest temperature registered was 25 F. and the number of nights when the temperature fell belovv 32, or freezing point, was 10. The rainfall was 1.35 inches, being about the aver- age that has fallen in the same month in the years 1886-7-8-9. Up to the present the rainfall only amounts to 8.56 inches from the 15th January. much below the average. The general direction of the wind has been easterly. SUMMER FASHIONS, now showing at I. &W. At a, meeting of the Committee on the 29th ult., the reports of the visitors for the month ended April 25th were read, and showed that the percentage of atten- dance was 83 as against 82 in the corresponding period of last year. div.head: TIIE NEW CODE.
div.p: TIIE NEW CODE.

The Clerk furnished the Committee with some parti- culars respecting the new code, especially with regard to evening schools, which will in future cease to be purely elementary in their character. Pupils who have passed the sth standard in the day school will be at liberty either to proceed to the higher standards, or to confine themselves to specific subjects, such as mathematics, mechanics, chemistry, French, shorthand, and other branches of scientific and commercial education, and the Board will be empowered to engage teachers duly quali- fied for these subject& The Committee recommended that the question of establishing evening schools should be considered by the Board, when the new code had passed into law.—The recommendation was adopted.

div.head: FEODSHAM PAEOCHIAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: FEODSHAM PAEOCHIAL COMMITTEE.

Mr. Lewis moved that the Parochial Committee for Frodsham and Frodshain Lordship be re-appointed and eonsiit of the same members as last year, and be invested with the same powers.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: t3EWBR OUTFALLS.
div.p: t3EWBR OUTFALLS.

Mr. Aaron moved that Mr. Wells, the special engineer to the anthority be requested to submit plans of the sewer outfalls of the district into the Ship Canal by next mee..ing.—Mr. Mclntyre seoonded. Carried. HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. , The Medical Officer reported that a death from typhoid fever had occurred at Frodsham. One of the children of the deceased, who was removed to the Workhouse some weeks ago, had developed the disease in the Workhouse. Two fresh cases of the same disease had also occurred at Netherton, the patients being Mrs. Challoner' and her son. A young boy had also been attacked at Claim Farm, Kingswood. As the parent was in the habit of carting his drinking water from Mrs. Challoner's farm, the supply at the latter place must be held accountable for both outbreaks. Orders had been issued for remedy- ing the defects which existed in connection with this water supply, and its use had been temporarily discon- tinued. In accordance with instructions, he had visited and inspected the closets and privy accommodation to the National schools at Helsby, and he was of opinion that they were defective and dangerous to health from their propinquity to the schools. Greater accommoda- tion was required and the site of the new structure should be considerably further away from the schools. He had also inspected the pig styes, on cottage premises known as Post Office Row in Alvanley, and he was of opinion that in their present condition they constituted a nuisance dangerous and injurious to health, but this might be remedied at slight cost if the yards were re- versed.—The Medical Officer reported verbally that a case of diptheria had occured at Newton by Daresbury. —The Nuisance Inspector said the analyst, had made an analysis of the water at Challoner's farm and he had returned it as a second class water and fit for domestic use.—Mr. Brandreth said when the Committee were at Helsby schools, the clo-ets were very filthy. He never saw anything worse in his life.—The Medical Officer said they were very inefficently looked after. He thmglit if a copy of his report were sent to the trustees of the school, they would take action. NUISANCE AT WESTON. A discussion took place as to a nuisance at Laalbsickle- lane, Weston, through the stoppage of a sewer ori land in the occupation of a man named Jones.—On the proposi- tion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Bra,ndreth, it was re- solved that seven days notice be given to Jones to open the sewer, in order to obviate the nuisance, and that if the notice be not complied with the Sanitary Inspector take out a summons and bring the matter before the magistrites. This was the whole of the business of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSE FUND.
div.p: RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSE FUND.

CONCERT BY TONIC SOL-FA CLASSES. With the object of aiding the fund for providing a district nurse for Runcorn, the present and past members of the Tonic Sol-fa classes gave a perform- ance of Root's popular cantata " David " in Runcorn Public Uall, on Wednesday evening. A capital audience assembled,and both the choir and the local vocalists who took the solo parts, were given unstinted prais'e for the careful and tuneful manner in which they performed the music. Mr. J. Holford conducted in his usual efficient style, and Mr. C. Le Couteux and Mr. H. Pope proved able accompanist, on the piano and harmonium respectively. During an interval in the programme Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., delivered an address in which he said the cause they were met to help forward had now got hold of their hearts. This was the Bth session of the Tonic Sol-fa Association of Runcorn; and he congratu- lated Mr. Holford, and he was sure they would also, upon the manner in which he had persevered in the work he had taken in hand in connection with that association. (Applause.) The music that had been performed that night was high testimony to Mr. Holford's Seeing that no outsiders had taken part. AU the solos had been sung by members from the ranks, and he thought that spoke highly for Runcorn. Applause.) Mr. Speakman alluded to the solace we derived from music after the business cares of the day were over, and went on to speak of the benefits that had been derived from the Education Act of 1870. Speak- ing of the Nurse fund, Mr. Speakman remarked that they ought to be proud of the nurse they had intheir midst, and he made that si-atement because it had been his good fortune to see a great deal of the work the nurse had done. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Holford had supplied him with the following facts which he thought ought to be made widely known. The most recent statistics ot the Education Department showed that in those departments where singing by note was taught,the tonic sol-fa method was used in 85.5 per cent. It had also been computed from these returns that there were 4.4 millions of child- ren in England, Wales and Scotland being taught to sing; 21 millions are taught to sing by note and of those 2.4 millions were tAught on the Tonic Sol-Fa method. It was also extensively used in the Middle and upper class schools. This concert marked the close of the eighth session of the Singing Classes at Runcorn. Since the classes commenced 510 persons had attended and 166 certificates had been gained, showing an average of 63 members and 20-75 certificates per session. This session the membership had been 84, and the certificates gained 39, so that both in respect to members and certifi- cates this had been the best session. (Applause).—The certificates were then distributed to the successful students and the concert proceeded.

The Deputy Clerk read a letter from the surveyor of taxes at Warrington, who informed the Board that they were liable to pay the sum of £5 3s. 9d. for income tax and bank interest for the past six years.—The Clerk said they had received interest from the treasurer for more than 20 years, and new the present surveyor said the Board were liable for income tax on the bank interest and he wanted to go back six years.—Mr. Parr: You will not pay it.—The Clerk said the treasurer was paid a Salary and the Board were allowed interest. He did not see how they were liable for income tax; the Board had no income. He suggested that they communicate with

the Inland Revenue on the matter.—Mr. Knowles said at Macclesfield the Guardians did not pay the treasurer a salary, and yet they received interest on their money.-- Mr. Brandreth proposed that the clerk write to the Macclesfield Board of Guardians in order to ascertain the conditions of their banking account with their treasurer. Stokes seconded the motion, which was carried.— The Surveyor of Taxes also wrote dip there was income tax to the amount of £2 las. Id. due for the past six Tears on the Sewage Tank Land.—Mr. Whitlow: I think they are short of work where that Comes from.—The Clerk said the proper persons to apply to in this matter , were the Aston Estate. Middlehurst said the subject of lunacy was an important one for Guardians and moved that copies of the Lunacy Act and the new regulations be obtained for the Guardians.—The motion was passed. hicraasEn WORK FOR THE CLERK.---. 1 letter was re- ceived from the Local Government Board dated the 30th April, stating that the form of financial statement required to be submitted ,by Boards of Guardians had been amended so that the statement might be a balancing statement, showing in greater detail than formerly the several items of receipt and expenditure, so that the en- tries in it might more clearly correspond with those

contained in the poor law returns.—The Clerk said this would necessitate a lot of extra work, and would also require new books of the stipulated form. THE ASSISTANT OVERSEERS, FOR ECCLESTON.—The Clerk said he had received a notice from Mr. George Hazlehurst Vie Government auditor, intimating that he had ad- journed the audit of the accounts of the township of Eccleston to Friday, the 13th inst. In reply to Mr. Mid- dlehurst the Clerk stated that the audit had been ad- journed in consequence of M. Parkinson, the collector, not having redeemed his promise to levy the rate, and collect it before the 25th March. The auditor had consequently given him until the period named in order to complete the work. ' AN ALLEGED DANGEROUS COLLIERY.—A letter signed "One that has seen children playing about it," had been received by the Clerk, in which attention was called to what the writer termed the dangerous and un- protected state of the old Bank Hay Colliery, at Sutton, and asking the Guardians to move in the matter.—The Clerk stated that the matter was not one for the Guar- dians—it was for the Town Council of St. Helens badeal with.—The Board decided that the communication should lie on the table. NEW SERVANTS.—MiSS Elizabeth Clarke, of Market Bosworth, was appointed assistant matron at a salary of £2O per annum, with rations, &c., and Miss Mary Don- nelly, of Chorlton, was appointed laundress, at a salary of LlB per annum. • This was the principal business.

RITNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday night. Mr. James Pritchard presided, and them were pre- sent the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, and Mr. A. Salkeld, with Mr.-G. Moss, clerk.

div.head: VININCE,
div.p: VININCE,

...... The Finance Committm leported that the amount in the treasurer's hands was £1,495 2s. 11d. Accounts amounting to £22 12s. 7d. were passed for payment. FOR THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S INFORMATION. Mr. T. B. Taylor (overseer) of Preston-o'-tle-Hill, ap- peared before the Board with regard to the death of Henry Ashton, which occurred in the Workhouse on the previous Wednesday. He said he gave the deceased and his son employment a few weeks ago. The Sunday after- wards they got a tittle drink, and were locked up. They were taken before Mr. Peter Stubs, who fined them, but gave them time to pay, but the "officer would not allow that" and he said they were only tramps. They were then sent to gaol, and the father, who was an old man, came back to his farm, and said" I am afraid they have killed me in that prison." lie was taken ill on the Thurs- day following, and he (Mr. Taylor) had him removed to tilt Workhouse on the Saturday. A doctor was not called in until Monday night. He wished to know whether any neglect occurred' in that House, and also what was the cause of the man's death; in order that he might give full information to Colonel Hamersley, the chief constable, and whom he intended to ask to make an inquiry.—ln reply to Mr. Stokes, Mr. Taylor said had he known the men were in custody he would have attended court on Monday morning and ad- vanced the amount of the- fines. Two better men he never had in his life.—The Clerk said the doctor had entered the causeof death as congestion of the lungs.— ,1 The Master said that when the man came to the House he seemed ill, and he sent him to the Hospital. The nurse attended to him, applied a poultice and the usual remedies, and she said she did not think it necessary to send for a doctor, as nothing more could be done for Grice said Mr. Taylor must be satisfied that there was no neglect in that House.—Mr. Taylor said lie was perfectly satisfied that there was no neglect in that House. The subject then dropped and Mr. Taylor , r >tired.

A RUNCORN PUBLICAN CONVICTED. Before Major Hazleburst and Dr. Steele, at Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Alfred Ellison, landlerd of the Man-at-the-Wheel beerhouse, Church-street, was summoned for having, on the 22nd April, unlawfully sold intoxicating drink to two drunken men named Thomas Carr and Thomas Kelly. Mr. J. Swift. barrister, of St. Helens, (in- structed by Mr. J. Burton), appeared for the defen- dant.—lnspector Bowyer said about a quarter to eleven on the night of the date mentioned he was in Church-street, and saw Thomag Kelly, lodging-house keeper, and two sailors, in a drunken state, staggering about the street. The men went into the Rose and Crown, kept by a man named Taylor, who, however, re- fused to serve them and they were out of the house into the street in less than a minute. They then went across the street and entered the Man-at-the-Wheel, kept by the defendant Witness, accompanied by P.C.'s Malkin and Brew,entered the house. The three men were stood at the bar, each with a glass of beer before him, and the man Carr was in the act of drinking. The Inspector said to Ellison " you see how drunk these men are, and you have gone and served them with more drink. They have been refused acrossthe road, and you have servea them." Ellison then said to the men " Why did you come into here. You have no respect for yourselves or for me, or anybody else." The Inspector told him he should report the matter, and the defendant said" I did not serve them; the missus served them." Kelly said he shoUld have his drink and seized his glass.— Ellison said" You shall not" and also seized the glass. Carr said "I have paid is. for um, and I shall have mine." The defendant then jumped over the counter and took the glass off Carr, whom he pushed outside. The other men had previously left the house. Carr was locked up and next morning he pleaded guilty to being drunk, and was fined as. 6d. and costs.—By Mr. Swift: He had cautioned the defendant a time or two. One night the defendant allowed a man to remain in the house a quarter of an hour after he was warned. There was one room in the house, that was frequented by very respect- able customers, but he was sorry to say the other was not. He had heard music and singing in the house, and he believed that loose women were not allowed there.— P.C.'s Malkin and Brew corroborated this statement.— Mr. Swift said the defendant had a seven years' lease in the house, which he had occupied for two years. He devoted tha whole of his time and attention to the management of the house, with the assistance of a bar- man named Scales. Mrs. Ellison resided in the domestic part of the premises, which are upstairs, and she scarcely ever interfered in any way with the management of the business or assisted at all. Upon the night in question there was no call upon her to interfere, and she had no authority from her husband, and her interference was altogether an unauthorised act upon her part, and did not earny responsibility to the shoulders of her husband. It had been erroneously supposed that a licensed victual- ler or beerhouse keeper was responsible for almost any- thing that was done in his house. He quoted a recent case in the Queen's Bench Division, to show that the judges held that a licensed victualler was not responsible for the unauthorised act of his wife. Between eight and half-past eight on the evening in question, two sailors, one of whom was Carr, entered the bar and wanted to be supplied with beer, but he refused, telling them that they had had enough. About half-past ten Mr. Ellison and the barman were in the bar parlour. and at that time there was nobody in the bar except two customers, of whom there was no complaint whatever. Mrs. Ellison came downstairs to speak to her husband, and seeing five men she asked what was wanted, and she placed the three glassesbefore the three men. At this moment the defend- ant came into the bar.and told his wife she had no business tq serve them, and they should not have it, as he had refused two of them two hours previously. Neither of the men paid for the beer, (whatever Carr may have said), and' the beer was tiever delivered, because the defendant stopped it.—The defendant, Mrs. Ellison, and the barman,named William Scales, gave evidence in sup- port of this statement. —The Bench retired to consider their decision, and on returning into Court fined the defendant 40s. and costs 14s. 6d. They would not en- dorse the license.—Thomas Kelly was then charged with being drunken the premises of the "Man at the Wheel." He pleaded not guilty. The inspector and officers proved the case, and the defendant called Mr. Ellison, who said if Kelly had entered the house alone, he would have served him With a pint. —A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed. -

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SODDEN DEATH OF CAPTAIN SCOTT.— Mr. Tibbits, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Commercial Hotel, Frodsham, on ihe body of Captain John Scott, aged 73 years, who had resided in Main-st.—Mrs. , Elizabeth Scott said the deceased, who was her husband, died on Saturday morning. The deceased came down- stairs about ten o'clock and complained that he did not feel very well. Afterwards he chopped some sticks, and at half-past eleven he said that pains had come in his chest again. He asked her to give him some spirits of camphor, hut she sent for Mr. Dunsford,who came to the house, and seeing that deceased was very ill, ordered some brandy to be given to him. Her husband at that time was quite conscious; the brandy appeared to do him no good, and other remedies were tried. Deceased fell down, and almost immediately expired.—Mr. F. W. Dunsford, chemist, said he recollected being called in to see the deceased. He was very ill ,and complained about a severe pain in the region of the heart, and was gasping for breath. Witness had known Captain Scott for two or three years, and had known that he had been suffer- ing from bronchitis; but he was not aware that he had a weak heart until Mrs. Scott informed him. When she described the symptoms he knew that he was suffering , from an affection of the heart. In witness's opinion, deceased died from heart disease. Dr. Robinson was called in to see the deceased, but he arrived after the man had died.—Dr. J. Robinson gave evidence showing that he had attended the deceased about twelve months ago for bronchitis. Deceased was suffering from heart dis- ease, and witness told him about it, and Captain Scott said he was aware of that. Witness attended the de- ceased until March, and saw him after his death. In his Opinion deceased died from heart disease.—The jury re- turned a verdict in accordance with medical testimony.

NEW NORTH WALES STEAMSHIP Co.—We understand that this company have decided to change the name of their steamer Cobra to that of the Saint Tudno, a dis- tinguishing name, which will at once associate this steamer with that part of Wales she is destined to con- nect by daily sailing's with Liverpool. The Saint Tudno, built by the Fairfield Steamship Co., is luxuriously ' fitted up and furnished with every modern comfort and convenience, including the electriclight, &c. The trip to Llandudno will he accomplished comfortably in two hours. The company have bean fortunate in securing the services of Captain Owen Lewis, so well known on this and other routes. An extra sailing, for the conven- ience of those spending the bank holiday in North Wales, and desirous of being at business on Tuesday morning, has been arranged. The St. Tudno will leave Menai Straits (Garth Ferry) cin Whit-Tuesday at 6.30 a.m., arriving in Liverpool at 9.30 a.m. There will also be a night trip from Liverpool at 8.30 p.m. on Monday, when the electric light will be used on board.
