div.head: WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY BILL.
div.p: THE WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY BILL.

This Bill, which seeks power to lay pipes from the centres of the brine supply inCheshire to the Widnes Alkali Works, where it can be dealt with in the usual way of manufacture,was considered on Thurs- day by a Select Committee of the House of Lords, under the presidency of Lord Basing. Mr. Littler Q.C.' Mr. Pembroke Stephens. Q.C. and Mr. Squarey were for the promoters. The Nortliwich Local Board were represented by Mr. Pope, Q.C., Mr. Freeman, and Mr. E. H. Lloyd; the Sincharn property owners by Mr. Clifford; the Cheshire County Council by Mr. Pember, Q C., Mr. Clifford, and Mr. Lloyd; the Widnes Local Board and the Bucklow Highway Board by Mr. Lloyd; the Manchester Ship Canal Company by Mr. Pember, and Mr. Noble; the Trustees of the Weaver Navigation by Mr. Pember and Mr. Clifford; and the Northwich Guardians by Mr. Balfour Browne, Q.C., and Mr. Marshall. . _

Littler, in opening the case for the promoters, said this was an entirely new proposal for the considera- tion of a Committee of Parliament. Their lordships would probably be aware that Widnes was a Lancashire town not without importance, and certainly not with- out smell. (Laughter.) It contained some of the largest alkali works in the world, and had the reputa- tion of being the greatest vegetable-killing place in the country. Salt was an absolute necessity in the manu- facture of alkali, and at present it had to be conveyed to Widnes, either as the common salt, which had again to be turned into brine, or as the rock salt, which also had to be converted for use. Alkali was formerly made by a costly process known as the Le Blanc process; but recently a much cheaper process had been discovered, the ammonia soda process, by which alkali was pro- duced, aspecially by Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., and unless Widnes was enabled to obtain the brine direct, her manufacturers would be most seriously han- dicapped. It was proposed to carry by pipes the brine from a pumping station near Northwich to Widnes. The ' Pipes would be laid along the public highway, except where they went through Sir R. Brook's land. If the scheme were passed, it would putan end to the abominable stenches,and all the destruction of vegetation would cease. He would call the chief inspector of alkali works to prove that no noxious gases would be emitted, and the present abominable waste would be prevented. The pumping station would be on a farm near to Northwich. The Widnes manufacturers could formerly get salt at 6s. 6d. per ton, but owing to the ingenious formation of the Salt Union the price had greatly increased. If a manufactur- er would agree to take salt from the Union for five years he would get it at 9s. 6d. ; but if he would only make the contract for two years he had to pay 12s. 6d. ; and if he would not bind himself at all he had to pay 14s. 6d. a ton. This increase in price had reduced the export trade in salt from 650,000 tons a year to about 400,000 tons; and it had, in addition, prevented the development of the home trade. The Bill would, therefore, emancipate Widnes from an outrageous monopoly. The opposition was not really that of the local boards nor of the occupiers, but of the limited companies, who were very much alarmed lest their monopoly should come to an end. The Salt Union at present carried thebrine in pipes to Weston Point, and the only difference between them and the promoters of the Bill was that the latter sought to cross the Mersey. The Salt Union were pump- ing day and night, and yet they wished to prevent other people doing the same, although the present proposal was only to draw the brine from 75 acres out of a bed of 250,000 acres in extent. Mr William Rock, chartered accountant, of Widnes, examined by Mr. Squarey, said he was one of the direc- tors of the promoting company. In 1888, prior to tie federation of the Salt Union, the net cost of salt to a Widnes manufacturer was 3s. 80. per ton, and the car- riage or; that was Is. 7d. Now the prices were under a five years' contract 9s. 6d. per ton; two years' cor, tract, 125.; and for a less period 14s. a ton. The Widnes manufacturers consumed 250,000 tons of salt a year. The increase in the price meant to them on the five years' contract £45,833 a year more; on the two years' £77,083 more; and otherwise it would mean £102,083 a year mere. This increase was due to the excessive pur- chase money paid under the Salt Union, who had a capital of £4,000,000, and the necessity for paying a dividend. Unless some such Bill as the one before the committee la ere granted, the Widnes manufacturers must either close their works or remove; at present they were not making a profit. Since the formation of the Salt Union the exports of salt had greatly decreased ; in the first three months of the present year the decrease was 17,368 tons. Cross-examined by Mr. Clifford: The Widnes manu- facturers wished to have better means of working, so that if necessary they might compete with Brunner, Mond, and Co. Then it would appear that Brunner, Mond, and Co. are, so to speak, running you off your legs ?—We want brine. In answer to Mr. Clifford, witness said it might happen that the taking of the brine to Widnes might lessen the rateable value of Cheshire. The promoters were merely looking after their own interests. They had paid £33,000 for the farm of 75 acres, and they proposed to arise £lOO,OOO by shares and £25,000 by debentures. Cross-examined by Mr. Marshall: In addition to the alkali works at Widnes there weresoap and copper works, and other manufactures. Their object in bringing the brine to Widnes was to sell it. They did not intend to manufacture. By Mr. Lloyd: There was no idea at present to carry the brine to St. Helens. In order that the brine might be of use to the Widnes manufacturers they would pro- bably have to adopt the new process. Mr. Mayer Cross, CE., said he was trustee of the Hutchinson estate, on which the major portion of the , Widnes works stood. He was of opinion that unless

they got brine to work the new process, the Widnes works would have to be closed because they could not compete. Be Mr. Marshall : He was of opinion that competition with the Northwich Alkali Works would reduce the cost of chemicals, and enable the Widnes manufacturers to "Mr. Thomas Snape, of the firm of Messrs. Thos. &tape and Co. alkali manufacturers, of Widnes, said that his works Used 7,000 or 8,000 tons of salt a year by the long process They had been considerably handicapped by the action of the Salt Union, who had rapidly put up. wises. The ammonia soda process was considerably the cheaper of the two, and brine was necessary for that , process. Brine had been found at Barrow, Fleetwood, and other places, and if alkali works were established there they would have a considerable advantage over ' Widnes. By Mr. Marshall: He only knew of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co. using the ammonia soda process in addition to Brunner, Mond, and Co. The latter were practically I the sole makers by that process. ' Mr. A. Fletcher, chief inspector of alkali works, was called to prove that the ammonia soda process would decrease noxious vapours in the manufacture of alkali. The ammonia soda process was a cheaper pro- cess than the La Blanc, and it generated none of the acids that arose from the old process. It could produce no injury to vegetation. By the diminution of evapora- tion from the salt pans in Cheshire,the atmosphere of the. district would be improved. Mr. A. Timmins, civil engineer, of Runcorn, stated the • results of the borings on the farm at Wincham pur- chased by the promoters. At'a depth of 162 ft. they reached the salt bed, and in 92 hours' pumping 60,000 gallons of brine were raised. This brine must previously have been flowing into the pits of the Salt Union. He , did not think that pumping on this land would cause sub- sidences at Northwich, as the level of the salt bed was- higher at Wincham than at Northwich. Mr. H. E. Taylor, C.E. of Chester, said he was en- gineer to the scheme. He did not understand that there was any special engineering difficulty in it. The reser- voir into which the brine would be pumped would con- tain two or three days' supply. Out of the 20 miles of pipes only two miles were petitioned against. Fer the first ten miles of pipes the brine would he pumped uphill , to the reservoir, and from that point to Widnes there would be a downward flow. He hadconstructeci simi- lar works for water supply. The welScs would supply 3,000,000 gallons of brine a week, or equal to about 3,000 tons of white salt. His estimate for the works was £30,500. Mr. Taylor, cross-examined by Mr. Pember, said it was not the fact that according to his sections the pipes would he much above ground. ,• The Chairman: Do you contend that it is in our power to carry your pipe 2ft. 6in. below the level Oe the road whatever that level may be a—Yes. The inquiry was adjourned. Yesterday morning, Lord Basing's committee further Considered the Widnes brine supply bill. The. obje,,-Aion Of the petitioners to the bill on the ground of the plaits being incorrect in detail, was discussed in private by the committee who had the assistance of the examiner of standing orders, and the legal adviser of the House of Lords. The chairman maid the committee was not pre- pared to throw outthe bill if proved to their satisfactton, on the ground of incorrectness of the sections' but they could only pass the preamble on c,ondition that amended sections were deposited before the third reading, Mr. Taylor the engineer of the scheme stated that clauses would he inserted to meet the objections of the Ship Canal Company in regard to the culvert trader the canal. The brine pipes would be carried over, the Mersey:four miles above Runnorn by a bridge the longest span of which would be 450 feet and they would be 75 feet above high water. The bridge which would cost £4,000 had been sanctioned by the Mersey Conservancy Board and the other river authorities. The committee subsequently adjourned until Tuesday.

div.head: HOW TO PROLONG HUMAN LIFE.
div.p: HOW TO PROLONG HUMAN LIFE.

A famous physician in France is now trying experi- ments with the object of prolonging human life beyond its natural span. His method is to introduce into the blood, in a peculiar form, the vital energy of the lower animals. Whether he will succeed or not we cannot tell, but it is very doubtful. So far men have foand only one way a securing a long life, and that is to prevent the organs of the body from becoming weak or torpid and of restoring to them their energy and power after they have partially lost it. That this, although difficult, has been done, and may be done, there is evidence to prove. But in all cases the work is performed in a very different manner from the one proposed by the French physician. Here is an instance in point :

Several years ago a woman—Mrs. William Crocker, of South Farmington, Nova Scotia—began to fail in health. Her symptoms puzzled her friends and herself. She had a good deal of headache; a bad taste in the mouth, cold hands and feet ; her skin took on a kind of yellow or coppery appearance, and she seemed dull, sleepy, and indifferent to things which had once inter- ested her. When walking she would occasionally be ob- served to stagger and catch hold of the nearest support to keep from falling. She was often sick, and vomited without apparent cause, and the bowels were tirregular and costive ; there was much heartburn and palpitation, and a rising of a hot and offensive wind or gas in the mouth and throat. In the autumn of 1884 she broke down completely. She complained of a sharp, cutting pain around the heart, and drew her breath with difficulty. There was a pain on the right side of the liver, and great distress and weakness low down in the small of theback, over the kidneys. Mrs. Crocker was put under the care of the best local physicians, who told bar that her case would prove hard to deal with, and gave her but small encouragement "All we can do," he said, " is to hope for the best." But three months' efforts were without favourable results. Her appetite was altogether gone, and how she lived was a wonder. She had now grown so nervous and excitable that she was afraid of the least noise, as a child is of the firing of a gun. Even common talking nearly sent her crazy. She had been plump and of good weight, but now her flesh was gone, and she looked like the mere spectre of the nobly-developed woman, once the envy of many. Seeing that no benefit came from the treatment she was receiving, another physician was employed, who put all his skill into the case for four months, and in all that time she never slept once, except under the influence of opium. Her condition was now such that she fervently desired to die, and her Dearest relatives agreed that she would be better off. Once in a while, however, the disease would seem to relax somewhat, and during these periods she could read for a few minutes at a time. It Was on such an occasion that, while glancing at a newspaper, her eye fell upon an article about a medicine called Mother Seig,el's Cura- tive Syrup. Fearing to be deceived she vet sent to St. -John's and bought a bottle, without mentioning to her doctor what she had done. On taking this medicine she was astonished and delighted to find it had an imme- diate effect. In a few days she could sleep without the opium, and was actually hungrya natural hunger. Food stayed on her stomach, and gave her scarcely any distress.

Full of hope and confidence she now avowed what she 'had done, discharged the physician, and sent to Halifax for six bottles more, and took it through the whole winter of 1884-5. The cure went steadily on, and in a few weeks, as she expresses it, "I felt as though I had •comeliack to life after having lain for months in -fin open grate :"

Ely the time spring set in she was able to do all her work. She is now sixty-three years old, fleshy as ever, enjoys life, and has every prospect of seeing an advanced age. In a recent letter Mrs. Crccker tells her story with an enthusiasm too warm for cold type, and says she owes her recovery to the mysterious medicine she saw advertised in the paper.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
DRUNK IN COURT.

On Saturday, a fustian cutter named Isaac Smith, who lives in Hopwood-st., was brought fip in custody at the Warrington Police Court. charged with having as- saulted his wife, and with having been drunk at the Police Court on Friday morning. The first case was dis- missed, but to the charge of drunkenness the prisoner pleaded guilty, and was fined ss. and costs.

div.head: NEGLECT OF FAMILY.
div.p: NEGLECT OF FAMILY.

Two cases in which men had left their wives and children chargeable to the common fund of the Warring- ton Union, were investigated by the Warrington borough magistrates, on Wednesday morning. William Allen, who was apprehended at Blackpool, and who is a stone- mason by trade, was brought up in custody on a charge of having deserted his wife and five child-fen. He left the town in December, 1888, and the maintenance of his family had caused the Guardians to incur an expenditure of £26 ss. 6d. Prisoner was ordered to go tq prison for a month, and to undergo hard labour. In the second case Jahn Dunn, a ropemaker, was charged in custody, on remand from the previous day, with having deserted his wife and child so far back as June, 1883. Ho was sent to jail for twenty-one days, with hard labour.

div.head: AN UNWELCOME VISITOR TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: AN UNWELCOME VISITOR TO WARRINGTON.

Annie Richardson, a middle-aged woman 'of bad char- acter, was before the IVarrington magistrates on Monday, on a charge of having been drunk in Arpley fields, on the day before. The evidence of a police constable was to the effect that prisoner, who was in company with sev- eral navvies, was guilty of disgusting conduct, in conse- quence of which she was taken to the lock-up. The Bench now committed her to prison for fourteen days, and the Chief Constable (M. Hunt) remarked to the magistrates that he hoped that the authorities would rmt pay her fare to Warrington when she was discharged. She did not belong to Warrington, but women of her class, who had been sent to prison by the magistrates, 'very often asked to be sent back to Warrington. In answer to the Mayor, Mr. Hunt said that prisoner be- longed to nowhere in particular, but was on circuit. When she was tired of one town she went to another. A LONDONER'S TIME,. AND WHAT IT COST RM. On Wednesday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a respectably-dressed young man, who gave the name of Thomas Morgan', and an address at 13, Fair- mead-road, Holloway, was charged with having travelled from St. Pancras to Warrington, without having purchased a ticket entitling him to do so. When the train due at Warrington at 5-30 in the morning arrived at the Central Station, prisoner was asked for his ticket. lie stated that he had neither ticket nor money, and was in consequence hapded over to the police. He now told the magistrates that he got into the train at Kentish Town, with the intention of going to Holloway, a die- tance of two miles, and that he fed asleep. A Cheshire Lines inspector, however, saidlhat the train in question, he believed, 41 not go to Holloway. Prisoner, who said that he ma wired to friends at Liverpool for assis- tance, was ordered to pay a fine of 10a. and costs, and also to pay the fare, 15s. iv. The alternative was 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: STEALING SHIRTS FROM A SHOP DOOR.
div.p: STEALING SHIRTS FROM A SHOP DOOR.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, two young men named Edwin Griffin and Thomas Martin were charged with having stolen three striped cotton shirts, value 7s. ed., from the shop of Mr. A. W. Paul, Horsemarket-st. ; and with having assaulted Constables Monaghan and Turner, in the Big Horse Shoe-yard, on Saturday night. Shortly after ten o'clock on Satnrday evening, the prisoner Martin was seen to snatch the shirts from a nail at Mr. Paul's shop door, and hand one or two of them to Griffin. Both prisoners then ran into the Big Horse Shoe-yard. Constablet Monaghan and 'Turner were told of the matter, and on going ,into the yard, found Martin wearing two of the stclen shirts and Griffin wearing the other one, in addition to their own shirts. Monaghan remarked," Well, how do they fit ?" Martin then rushed at him, and tried to knock him down, and Griffin assaulted Turner. A scuffle _ensued. but the police officers managed to hold their men until, other constables arrived, when the prisoners were taken to the bridewell.—Griffin was sent to prison for two months' hard labour for the robbery, and one month for the assault; and Martin was committed for a month on each charge. Tomark their disapproval of the practice of hanging goods outside shop doors, the Bench did not allow the owner of the stolen property any costs.

div.head: FIIT.MY way OF SHSIIVING AFFECTION.
div.p: A FIIT.MY way OF SHSIIVING AFFECTION.

William Roberts, a canal rnn.n, who lirßs at 4, Rose and _crown-street, was brought before the Warrington maz-is- trates on Tuesday, on a charge of having assaulted his wife, Elizabeth Roberts. She said that on Sunday morn- ing he, without any provocation, struck her twiceon the head and kicked her several times. He was sober at the time. Replying to the prisoner, she denied that she first threw a teacup at him, giving him a black eye. Pri- soner said that the complainant was not his wife. She was in the habit of leaving him for weeks at a time, and that was the cause of all the mischief. She went away, and then came back and kicked up " wops." Mr Robert Garnett pointed out that if the complainant was not his wife the prisoner was not compelled to keep twr.

—Prisoner: I know I'm not oblP,ed to keep her; but love the ground that woman walks upon. (Laughter./ —Mr. Garnett: You have a funny way of showing it.— Prisoner: I did strike her; but she struck me with a teacup.—Mr. Garnett : If you lore the ground she walks upon, you would rather enjoy it than otherwise. (Laughter.)—Prisoner said he had served through the Crimean War and the Indian Mutiny, and had a good character.—Complainant asserted that she was married to the prisoner at Qibraltar, and had borne him sixteen children.—The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs.

div.head: 3IURDEI AT DUDLEY.
div.p: 3IURDEI AT DUDLEY.

The Dudley police have arrested four men on a charge of causing the death of Thomas Cartwright, labourer, of Tipton. On Saturday night Cartwright went tc, Dudley Theatre, and on leaving was set on by a gang of roughs, who knocked him down and kicked him. He sustained severe Injuries. which necessitated his removal to the Guest Hospital,where he died. Cartwright was 19 years of age.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A YOUNG WOMAN.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A YOUNG WOMAN.

On Monday afternoon Martha Massey, 21 years of age, a domestic servant committed suicide by drowning herself in the Sankey Canal, near War- grave. The young woman's pqrents resident Button- wood, but she had been employed at the house of Mr. J. Riley, greengrocer, Market-st., Earlestown, for some time past. She left Mr. Riley's on Monday and after visiting her home, stated that she had secured another situation at the Griffin Inn, Earle-st. The de- ceased, however, did not visit the Griffin Inn, but was next seen walking along the canal towing path. A man named Bridge who was working in one of the fields in the vicinity suddenly saw her throw her umbrella into the water after which she herself jumped in. Bridge immediately gave an alarm, but she had dis- appeared before anyone arrived at the spot. Informa- tion was at once given to the police authorities, and Police Constables Cameron and Bowes recovered the body after a brief search. The unfortunate girl still held by the string a small parcel ;containing some clothing. The body was removed to the.Wargrave Inn. . . . .

. An mquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, at the Wargrave Inn, on Wednesday. The evidence was to the effect that the deceased left her home at Burtonwood about three o'clock on Monday afternoon, p.nd informed her mother and her sister that she was going to a situa- tion as domestic servant at the Griffin Inn, Earlestown. She did not go the Griffin Inn,however, but was seen to throw himself into the canal as stated. The deceased had been discharged from a previous situation and this was considered to have preyed on her mind. A verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind "was returned.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS RECREATION.

With a view of giving the Warrington Gymnasium a helping hand, a match was arranged for its benefit on Saturday, sanction having been obtained from the Rugby Union. Recollections of the previous fine /displays be- tween theabove clubs, and the interest taken in the meetings by their supperters, ef which no clubs in the County Palatine have more staunch ones, the Warring- ton executive adopted a wise course in bringing the famous St. Helens club to the Wilderspool enclosure, and at the time of kicking off there would be fully 13,000 people present. Previous to the match the local eight, who performed' so well in the-recent- gymnastic display at Liverpool, gave an exhibition of club, barbell, dum- bell, and parellef bar exercises, and no doubt to this was largely due- such a numerous attendance. Their display was of a unique description, and each item was loudly applauded. It was an hour after the advertised time when the Rees, stepped into the field,. closely. for- lowed by Warrington, each team beingawarded a' hearty reception. Both sides suffered from and War- rington losing the toss, defended,the-railway goal: Frank Turner's kick off was responded to by Sedden, and from the first pack formed 'Frank Turner- dribbled finely, the prompt and plucky saving of Ellisonstopping his progress, A moment later Evans almost get in.after a fine dodgy run,, and the Recs. only managed to clear by the aid of strong forward play and judicious kicking. The Warrington quarters were entered after ten minutes' :play, and after Jackson and Dram. had ' ems:hanged kieks, a fine piece of work by Webster placed his side :on the aggressive, play- being in close proxiinity 'the pavilion goal. Bate dodged away. from -a pack! and I finally threw to Webster, who get over- the line, but ,on his endeavour to gain the coveted try he had unfor- ,tunately stepped into touch and the point was made void. Stiff scrimmages-and a successionofline-outs were carried on here, until Rowe and Berry dribbled over the line, and Seddon conceded the first minotto Warrington. Neutral ground was- the scene of play immediately after the dropout had been effected, and from allimesaßater Bandies, and Massey passed finely, bat the effort weal negatived when Mousdale, Part, and Fildes headed afor- ward movement to the home line, Bosco's- defendingliis.l charge in capital style. Seddon essayed a drop at•goal,. but Evans was exceptionally clever, and frustrated the effort. The Saints were now having decidedlY the best of it, and had Warrington showed any signs of' submit-' ting to the oppressien, the Recs, must have scored. But all the " wirepullers' "Old vigour was railed "upon, and not hi vain, and's-fang kick by Boscowy follbwed by- 'grand passing movement be the Warrington hirwardar caused Jackson some anxiety, his coolness at this jime• hire serving him tb advantage. After-the•llecs.• hatf forced a minor some fine work by Jolley, E. Dillon, and 1 Berry tobk the leather to the Saint' a post, and Jackson ,saved. From some short' passing between Bate and ! ROwe Evans tried a shot at goal, and the ball goingwids I a third minor was credited to. Warrington, which latter ' item brought the firstlialf to a-close, the score standing Warrington, 0-OZ-; St. Helens, PM' Seddourestarted, Jolley responding to the kick-off' in touch'. at the half,. way flag. After an exhibition of exchange frielcitig,.in which neither side could claim a distinct advantage, a lone succession of scrimmages followed, which' rendered the game of a monotonous description. Monsdaleat length passed finely to Ellison, who kicked to Beseow, but the Warringtoman was exceptionally safe. and never made the semblance of a mistake. Frank Ttirner and Berry dribbled 'finely, and Massey had an openins,;.but a pass forward spoiled the chance. However, Bate • got away from the ruck, and Massey and Randles passed finely and half way again saw play being contested. Massey and Seddon exchanged kicks, and altheug,h,the last-named had a rare chance affOrded him a:moment later, the tackling was sure,. and the pressure staved off. Passlng by the Saints ultimately' - ended in a minor. Rowe came in for special notice immediately after the drop out, -and then ensued a capital display be- tween Jackson and Webster, both players coming in, for well-merited applause. A .fine passing movement be- tween Rowe, Frank Turner, and Donohue took the-game near the Saints' line, and from a return kick near the 'half-way flag. Webster took the oval at top • speed,. and pushing Ellison at one side he ran to the line, .where- the safe clutches of Jackson brought an end to hiS- deter- mined attempt to give his side, the lead, a touch, in goal being the result Bate and Fair • Turner- each in turn showed up prominently, but strive as eaeh side. did, no major point was scored; and when. the • vrhistle. sounded "No side" the final result was a draw,. the. 5C01,2 then reading—Warrington four. minors, .St. Helena-Recreation two minors.

The result was a 'fitting ending to so even a game, and from start to finish victory was in the balance. The dis- play given by both teams was, however, not Ora. taking description, as the brunt of the work fell to the la of the forwards and it certainly became- monotonous: Tndivi- dually, iOSCOVF stood out prominently in the home backs, and Warrington are to be complimented onpossessing so safe a custodian. Webster plays better at three-quarter than full back; and the couple of efforts he made during the match when he-was pullet up on the line- served to Drove that had he received more work- a, major point would certainly have been registered. Massey had little to do, and Evans was well watched by Seddon. Both Bate and Rowe have been seen to better advantage, and of the forwards Frank TUrner, Berry,. and Ranches were the pick.

The Everton P.C. lost only nine ont of 61 engage- ments. Only once were their colours lowered at home, and that by the North Did. This, however, was after- wards avenged, followed by another decisive victory over the League champions during the past week. Ever- ton scored in every match except one, whilst they kept their own goal intact on no fewer than 21 occasioas. Everton are also far in advance of any club in the king- dom as regards scoring goals. Up to the end of April they had totalled 275 to M. This gives them a splendid average, being close on the heels of Queen's Park, who, however, have only gone through half as many fixtures.

ALARMING FIRE AT ABRAM GOT.T.TRRIES. About half-past nine on Wednesday morning a fire, which did a great amount of damage, broke out in the engine-house of the Arley Mine, belongav to the Abeam Coal Company, Bickk,shaw, near Leigr4 The collieries are the largest in the district. Work on Wednesday Morning was commenced at six o'Cloc•and windkig operations went on as usual to about the time.stated above, when the en:Tine-man, John Leadbetter, was startled by seeing a Aline burst from the drum upon which the ropes attacifid to the cages arrwound. The fire spread with alarminzrapidity,and Leadbetter had to beat a hasty retreat through one of the whitlows in the rear of the engine-hotre-,-the roof of whichtWas quickiy alight. Before the fit- 'could be extaguished the. machinery was much' ' damaged, and, through the snapping of one of thrwinding ropes, ore-of the cagee- tellto the bottom of the shaft. This naturally caused alarm below, but the memand boys in the mint, number— ing 320, were quickly reassured, and weze as soon as, possible brought to the surface.

THE RECTORY OF WINWICK.

INDUCTION. Or THE NEW RECTOR. The induction of the Rev. Canon Penrhyn as' rector of Winwick, ia succession to the late Rev- Canon Hopwood. took place at Winwick Church on Thursday afternoon. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Canon Whitley, MA., rural dean, and amongst those present on the occasion, in addition., to the new rector, were—The Rev. J.. Carson (Mr' ate-in-charge), the Rer-E. C. E. Carleton, Captain VVithington, Mr. Joseph Swinton, and Mr. J. E• Worsley ( churchwardens), Mr. Thomas Warburton (sidesman), Mr. Charles Whitley, Mr. George Powl- son, Mr. Elvin, Mr. R. Stone, Mr. Cooper,' Mr. Clarke, Mrs. Carson, Misses Comber, Min Worsley, Mrs. Longton, &c. A little - after three o'clock in the afternoon the church was cleared of spectators and tile' north door of the church was locked by the churchwardens, who then handed the key to Canon Whitley. The Canon then grasped the hand of the new , rector and placing it on the key read the following :• ; "By virtue of this (the Bishop's) mandate I induct you linto the real, actual, and corporal possession of the Ret- tory of Winwick in the dioceseof Liverpool, with all its • fruits, members, and appurtenances," Canon Whitley !then handed the key to Canon Penrhyn, who thereupon ' opened the doer, entered the Church, closing the door be' hind him, and tolled one of the bells 22 times. Thls being considered by the inducting clergyman as sufficn- • cut, he bade the Rector cease,, which the latter at once did, and admitted the spectators into the church. The ' party next proceeded to the vestry where the Bishop tificate of induction was witnessed by Canon Whitley, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, the Rev. James Carson. the churchwardens, and Mr. Robed Stone, and Mr. C. T. Cooper. This concluded the. ceremony. On Slinday Canon Penrhyn will read and declare his adhesion to the Thirty Nine Articles, which declaration will terminate the induction formalities. PROPOSED MEMORIAL TO ,THE LATE RECTOR.' It has been decided by a number of parishioners and 1 friends of the late Rector of Winwick (the Rev. canon 1 Hopwood) to perpetuate the memory of the deceased clergyman by the erection of a stained glass window in Winwick Church. The window is estimated to ute,t £250, and a design has been approved by the late Canon! • family. The window is to be placed on the south side oi thechurch near to the belfry. The following subscriptions have been already received :—Colonel McCorquodale £l° lOs.; Mrs. Comber, £lO 10s. ; Mr. T. Comber,\ £lO 10s. • Mr. G. Comber, J.P., £lO 10s. ; Mrs. S_terl'* • and family, £lO 10s. Mr. Robert Stone, £5 55.; ssr6' - McCorquodale £2 2s. •- Dr. Watkins £1 Is. div.p: .A(GIPaYiBOUNDLING'S CA:MOIL

The name ofJohn Warrington, a youth,whoissme four or, five years,ago, earned a good deal of -.noto- riety, was mentioned at the Warringion ,Board of Guardians on Wednesday. Warrington .was posed to be of gipsy parentage,and as an infant.was deserted in the neighbourhood of Warringtoarand When 'found, take.n to the workhouse. As he grew Up it, of course, became necessary to label him,,with a name, and he received that of the town in ,which be had been reared. He soon began to display a full Proportion of the *wandering propensities of ancestors, and often scaled the walls both at the Woritti house and at Padgal.e schools and generally disappeareW for a few days on each Occasion, sometimes playing; rather ventuiesorne pranks while at large. He was at length consigned to the ship " Clio," and the occasion of. his name coming before the Guardians on Wednesday was the fact that he had been, by order of the Home SeerefarY.opusigned to Denbigh Asylum. The asyluin, authorities had written asking the Guardians to pay for the lad's maintenance. he liability for this was not admitted by the Guardians, and the Clerk (Mr. j. C. Sutton) remarked that this was the first case they liad had under the new lunacy. ~and it was rather singular that the act, which had over ZOO clauses, did not provide for it. They could see, therefore, that there was room for law and litigation. The Guardians desired that the Clerk should endeavour to ,come to some amicable arrangetnent with the Denbigh Asylum authorities.

div.p: • WARRINGTON BOARD .OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board VMS held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Alder- 19,_au Harrison presided, and there were also present *--ne Revs. G. F. Roberts, and R. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. 11. ..rd (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (super- kutendent of Patigate Schools). THE WARRINGTON DEATX-RATZ. The CLERK reported that an exceptional and a serious ieature of registration in the past quarter was the pay- of fees in respect of 399 deaths, and 4,83 births, in e town of Warrington. The numbers for the corres- Ponding quarter of 1889 were 235 deaths and 501 births. It was difficult to fix an increase of population as the cause for the increase of mortality, seeing diat;the deaths .;ver°He 164 more and the births 18 less. In the nine years ewing the census of 1871 the annual increase of births Z:inecireda s e° a of s proved in ratio to each other, and also to the population in the decade, as shown by the CR118" or 1281. The quarterly averages had shown a roPortional excess of births over deaths. The quarterly averages for the nine years at Warrington were 382 births - kud 208 deaths. From a return given him by the master be found the number of deaths at the Workhouse in the Wt four corresponding or first quarters to have been 47, 28, and 30, so that the Workhouse death-rate did nut seem to account for the increase. div.head: HONE WILE CONFEUNCE.
div.p: HONE WILE CONFEUNCE.

At the Scottish-Welsh Home Rule conference in London, on Tuesday, resolutions were passed to, the effect that in a .final settlement of the Home Rule question, a legisdature:should be granted to each of the four nationalities—England, Scotland, Ireland, and Wales—for the management of local affairs,still main- taining the suprecnacy .of the Imperial Parliament, in which each nationality should be represented. A Committee was appointed to carry out the ,bbovo resolu- tion.

div.head: END OF IRISH RAILWAY STRIKE.
div.p: END OF IRISH RAILWAY STRIKE.

Work was resumed on Monday mornittlr by the work- men' employed on the Great-Bouthern and Western Rail- way, Ireland, and goods and passenger traffic is now 1, fully re-established. Sotoe small places on the line have suffered seriously for want of .supplies. At Nenagh the tradesmen's stock of flour andocalhadbecome exhausted, and arrangements had been made to convey fresh sup- plies from Limerick by road,. Archbishop Walsh has written to the " Freeman's Journal "suggesting that the Coßaoration and the Chamber of Commerce should take steps to constitute a Board of Conciliation for the settle- ment of trade disputes, and the prevention of strikes and j lockronts.
THE REV. A. A. DIGNUM AT SALEM, .INDIA.

The •"%Vycliffe Church Record" for May, has the following extract from the report of the Rev. A. A. Dignum, just received :—" During the year I have spent about one hundred and eighty days in the district, visiting the out stations and preaching in the villages. At least half of this time was devoted to the work in Atar, where not only have we the largt st number of Christians, but also where the people gene- rally show a more attentive and intelligent interest in our work. In June I was accompanied by ttak Revs. M. Phillips and O. G. Marshall ,in a lon* tour through this part of the district, in the course of which we visited about fifty villages and preached to over seven thousand people. Wherever we went, we had large and attentive audiences, and as evidence of the interest of the people, it may be mentioned that our sale of tracts and portions of Scripture exceeded in value Rs. 20, representing about fifteen hundred booklets. In one,of the large towns, a Brahmin official welcomed us to his house, and hospitably provided didner for us an act of courtesy which was as surprising as it was pleasing, for according to his sas- trams, our presence in his house must have polluted it. In Atfir Mr. Phillips addressed a large audience in Eng- lish on the Spiritual Telescope. Occasionally I have visited the village, near to which I have been encamped, after dinner at night, and at such times have invariably secured large audiences, the headman providing mats for us to sit upon, and getting the people to sit down and listen quietly to our singing and addresses. In two or three of the larger towns I have exhibited the magic lantern to large crowds, and in the year upon which we have entered, I intend to use this means of presenting the Gospel to the people much more largely than hitherto. In two or three villages near Sankerry Droog, there are several farmers who have given up idol worship, and are reading the Bible and receiving regular instruction from the catechist. Already, in this part, we have several con- verts frona the Shudra class, and this fact accounts for the willing reception of our message in the neighbour- hood."

_ THE DEPOTS AGAIN.

_ Sir,—With the approach of warm weather, we are beginning to feel the foul smell which proceeds from the Corporalion depot in Hardy-st. Already we have written the Sanitary Committee on the subject, and we beg to enclose the correspondence for insertion in the .Examiner."—We are, yours faithfully, PRO -EDWARD BOLTON & SONS. J. F. Orford-lane Glass Works, Warrington, 9th May, 1890.

The Chairman, Sanitary Committee, Town Hall, May 5, 1890. Sir,—We beg again to call your attention to the nuis- ance and dreadful smell arising from the denet in •Orford-lane, opposite our property. To-day, from 12 o'clock and now at the moment of writing 4.15 p.m., it ,is very bad, and would not be allowed on private pre- mises very long. We have plenty of witnesses to prove this.—Yours truly,
E. BOLTON AND SONS.

Town Clerk's Office,. Warrington, May 7, 1890. Dear Sirs,-1 am directed by the Sanitary Committee to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the sth inst., and to inform 3rou that your complaint is entirely un- founded, as the delibt in Hardy-St. was not working on the day you allege the nuisance existed, and was in fact locked up.—Yours truly,
J. 1..T0N WHITTLE. Messrs. E. Bolton and Sons, Glass. Manufacturers, Orford-lane.

Sth May, 1890. Dear Sir,—We have your favour of the 7th just, in acknowledgment of our communication of the sth of the same, and must express our surprise and disappointment .at the off-hand manner in which you dispose of our com- plaint. As we presume neither you nor the Sanitary Committee were at the depot in Dardy-st. the time we .referred to, we cannot see how you could say our com- plaint was "entirely unfounded." And further, your 'curt reply was anything but courteous to us, as rate- payers who have to contribute our share of taxation for sanitary purposes. Indeed, we might not be very far wrong in regarding it as a wanton insinuation against -our veracity. Whether the depot was working or locked up was a matter with which we have no concern. In •either case it is a standing nuisance, and we claim pro- .tection from the abominable stench which it spreads through the whole neighbourhood. We shall not let the matter drop.—Yours faithfully, EDWARD BOLTON & SONS. .Mr. J. L. Whittle, Town Clerk, Warrington.

" MORE FACTS!' *nr,—l have no very particular desire to enter upon 1" discussion on the various points of faith and practice of Catholics," though I am tolerably familiar with them. It was to save my fellow townsmen and country people attending our parish churches from being blindly led into the adopt-ion of some of the many errors of the Romish Church, that I first wrote to you, and on that occasion I stated a few facts,which your correspondent "Thomas Williamson" wishes to make out are no facts at all. I, 'however, deny that rhave made any false assertions re- garding his belief, or that I have any misunderstanding ,as to his religion. What I asserted was, that on the con- tinent there is no mention of Christ—meaning, of course, as The Christ—but that the great object of the Catholic worshippers, was the Virgin Mary. That this is so is borne out on all Mts. Why, immediately a Catholic approaches a French port, be be ever so much troubled with sea sickness, he crawls up on deck and goes through a pantomimic performance in front of a huge representation of the Virgin. I also stated, what your correspondent denies, that Catholics also worship saints, crucifixes, and images. Now, it is very evident that Mr. Williamson and I differ very materially as to the meaning of this word " worship ' but, when I see people act as above stated, when I also see them buy candles, light them, stick them pn a rack, and then go and kneel before a representation of a saint, bow repeatedly and make prayers, I am forced to the simple and irrestible conclusion that all this is worship and idolatry. Then your correspondent sets up the mother of Christ as the mother of God, and says we are to honour her because Christ honoured her. But Christ simply hon- oured His mother as we all, I trust, honour our own mothers, and not with any such honour as amounts to worship, nor does De anywhere command His followers to give her special honour. Mr. Williamson advised us also to read the Bible, but when I point out that the Bible does not favour his views, he calmly seeks to go beyond the Bible and pleads tradition. But even this tradition was condemned by Christ himself (Matt. xv. 2-8 ; Mark vii., 8), and by the Apostle Paul, who was once very valiant in its defence. (Gal. i., 13.14). An old writer says "that the best mode of defending the dogmas of Rome is to weaken men's respect for the authority of the holy scriptures," and this your correspondent essaysobut I remind him that the Bible is thebest book that was ever written against Popery, and I hopeyour readers will take Mr. William- son's advice respecting it and read it for themselves. For maintaining their errors, the Catholics have been forced, says an early writer, to devise "a new rule," never owned by the Primitive Church ,nor by the ancient Court- I cils, of adding to the word of God the traditions of their I Church. Your correspondent quotes from Macauley a seemingly favourable passage, but forgets to add the writer's conclusion on the subject. In conclusion I hope your readers will search the scrip- tures,and if they only follow out its precepts they will see there is no need to draw the nice distinctions that Mr. Williamson draws in the practise of his religion, and that they can come direct to God himself without the mediation of saints,crucifixes, or images. By so doing they willpossess a better and more abiding peace than the Catholic Church can ever bestow—a peace that passeth all understanding.—Yeurs, &c., A DISSENTER.

ROMAN CATHOLICS AND THE VIRGIN MARY. Sir,—I have read the letter of your corresponpent, Mr. Williamson, and can only conclude that either he is not familiar with the full teaching of his own Church : or else he desires to blind Protestants to what that teaching really is. He asserts that "Catholics do not give the Blessed Virgin divine honours which belting to God." Now, from Scripture we are distinctly taught that prayer is a part of that worship, or'' divine honour" which is due to God alone. The Roman Church sanctions prayer to the Virgin Mary; therefore she is giving divine honour due to God only. The emphatic promise is "Whatso- ever you shall ask the Father in My (Jesu's) name he will give it you." Neither example nor precept sanctions prayer to Mary; or prayer to the Father through Mary. Yet in opposition to the manifest teaching of the Bible, Rome teaches that she may receive what God alone is entitled to. In a word, divine worship is given to the Virgin. This is not assertion, but fact. Now for the proof—petitions of exactly the same kind :and wording as those addressed to God, are offered to Mary. The " Raccolta" consists of a collection of prayers specially indulgenced by Popes, hence, it is of indis- putable authority. Herein we find such language addressed to Mary—" Save me, my Hope; save me from Hell." " Sweet heart of Mary, be my salvation." "We fly beneath thy shelter, 0 itoly Mother of God, despise not our petitions in our necessities, and deliver us always Irons all perils." Next, in the "Glories of Mary," by St. Liguori, we have direct prayer to the Virgin ; and re- member that the Roman Church has decreed that all the writings of Liguori are faultless. What it contains the Church of Rome approves of and sanctions. There we read—" 0 Mother of Mercy, appease thy beloved Son," "We beseech thee, prevent thy beloved Son, &c." And we are told that "To her belong dominion and power over all creatures" that " often we shall be heard more quickly if we have recourse to Mary and call upon her name, than if we should call upon the name of Jesus." , "Mar)- is our only refuge, help, and asylum," whilst the very last words which the Roman ritual puts into the mouth of the dying, are, "Mary,- mother of grace, mother of pity, do thou protect me from the foe, and re- ceive me in the hour of death." Again in the "Breviary," which priests must daily read, we find, "Receive what we present, comply with what we request, allow for what we fear : for thou art the only hole of sinners." Amongst hymns in Mary's honour, we read— '0 holy Mother of our God. To thee for help we fly; Despise not this our humble prayer. But all our is ants supply."

' Further Cardinal Bellarmine says "that saints are to be prayed to " ; and Azorius admits that they do give "divine 'worship" to saints; whilst the Cathechism of Trent says that" to pious minds no doubt on the subject can occur" that " prayers are made" to the saints; and the Council of Trent condemns such as deemed it foolish to "supplicate, verbally or mentally" saints in heaven— Rome authoritatively sanctions prayer to saints departed; and as idolatry consists in giving the creature what only is due to the Creator, she sanctions idolatry. As if aware of this she strikes out of a majority of her Catechisms the second commandment. Well may we ask, what want we with Mary's advocacy with Scripture so plain. "if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ," and He declares "lam the way, no man cometh unto the Father but by Me"; and invites" Come unto me all ye that labour and are heavy laden." , That saints cannot hear prayer is the testimony of the Bible. That the whole thing is a novelty appears from what Cardinal Peirin says, "No trace of the invocation of saints can be found in the authors who lived nearest to the the times of the apostles " ; and that there exist.. "No footsteps of this praying to saints, either in scrip- ture, or in the Fathers before the first four Councils." When we first find the worship of the Blessed Virgin appearing, it was challenged, and condemned as a novel heresy. The great Christian Doctor, St. Epiphanius, _ 403, A.D., warns that she "was not given to us for worship " ; and exhorts "Let no man worship Mary."— I remain, &c.,
TRUTH.

div.p: ROMAN CATHOLICISM.

Sir,—As "Runcorn Redtail "accuses me of only reading literature favourable te my opinions, I think he must indeed be very dull of comprehension seeing the quotations I have made and whichhave not been disproved. He says Mr. Williamson has made a sensible defence of Romanism, a thing impossible to defend. The Tractarians in the Church of England, many of whom are only Papists in disguise, adopt the same theory. I proceed with proofs; the scripture passages I take from the Romish version. Surely this should suit "Redtail "and "Mr. Williamson." Tradition is not wanted, for it will not bear scrutiny in very many cases. The Council of Trent, reg. four, says—" If any man should dare to read or have a Bible without license from the bishop or inquisitor, he shall not be capable of absolution, unless he part with his Bible." Search the Scriptures (John 5c.) "But though we or an angel from heaven preach a gospel to you besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema," (Gal. lc.) "Dearly beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God; because many false prophets are gone out into the world," (1 John 4c.) "But prove all things: hold fast that which is good," (1 Them. 5c.) Search and prove all things and try the words of the teachers, is opposite to what Cardinal Newman says, namely, "The Church cannot allow her children the liberty of doubting the truth of her word." What is found in the Romish Missal on the Mass? I have it before me. "Sprinkle holy water before solemn mass, the priest at the foot of the altar, confess to God, Virgin Mary, Michael the Archangel, Holy of Holies (the chancel) 0 Lord by the merits of thy saints, whose relics are here, and of all the saints, that thou wouldst vouch- safe to forgive me all my sins." Not a word about holy water, altar, cnnfessing to saints, or merits of relics, to be found in Matt. 26c., Mark 14c.,Luke 22c., 1 Cor. 11c., where the words of the institution of the Lord's Supper are to be found, and in these places only. Christ called it a table. The disciples sung a hymn, not prayed to Saints, Virgin Mary, or pleaded the merits of any relics. It was in an upper room, not an elaborate chancel as Romanists and Ritualists call it the" Holy of Holies." A table is for ministers not for priests. The Romanist never takes the Lord's Supper because his church, the priests, deny hi en the wine, although Christ said, "Drink ye all of this." Matt. 2ec., " And they all drank of it," Mark 14c. Saint Paul particularly urges the laity to partake of the cup, 1 Cor. 11c. The laity had the wide up to Council of Constance, A.D., 1414 (see " Romanism weighed" by Di. W. Preston, of Runcorn, page 250). I advise " Redtail" to get a copy, or Bishop Mant's Churches of England and Rome compared, printed in parallel columns, price fourignee. This will not make "Redtail" hantrupt.l pranise him, if he will only read i thoughtfully, his eyes will be opened. If he prefers the "Glories of Mary," a book highly commended by Cardinal ManMng ; he may possibly get a copy for about eye shillings. For his edification I give him a few extracts "Jesus, Mary and Joseph may I breathe forth my soul unto you in peace "--300 days' in- dulgence, by decree of Pope Pius VIII., April 28, 1807. Christ said "Thou shalt adore the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve;' Luke 4c Bv. "To thee do I this day consecrate my whole soul," p 116. Saint Paul differs in Romans 12c Iv. Thou (Mary) art the only hope of sinners—Breviary Office for Sept 9. Christ Jesus our hope, 1 Tim lc. "Oh! Lady in heaven, we have but one advocate, and that is thyself," p 168 The beloved dis- ciple John said—" But if any nfan sin, we have an advo- cate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the just," 1 John 2c lv.—l leave your readers to judge of " Redtail's " views of Mr. Williamson's sensible defence. In the "Garden of the Soul" I read—" The person that is to receive the Blessed Scrament must be fasting, a. least from midnight, by the command of the church" (i. 9 the parsons). What saith the Scriptures—" But when it was evening not morning) and whilst they were eating (not fasting) Matt. 26. In the same book, I find —"St. Helen, most holy queen and mother of the first Christian emperor, pray for England," and in the Rosary of the Blessed Virgin Mary I find the Lord's prayer is to be said once and "Hail Mary" ten times. Latria is the highest form of worship in the Romish Church, and it is to be given to the wafer or as it is called Host; Council of Trent, Bess. 13. Thomas Aquinas de- clares—" That the image of Christ is to be adored with the adoration of Latria. ' In the Roman Pontificial we find as follows, "The cross of the legate, because 'atria is owed to it, shall be onthe right hand." In the "Catholic Times" of April 25 last there is the follow- ing from the Lady Abbess of Chudlegh, Devon, that "Christ himself appeared to Saint Bridget of Sweden in the 14th centiiry." At the feast of Portiuncula, held in , St. Joseph's Church, Grosvenor-st., LiverpooLon August Ist last, an Indulgence was to be given in following terms—" Confession and holy communion, visit St. Joseph's, prayer for the Pope's intention. To gain this five "paters." and five "hail Mary's" are sufficient; one visit will obtain one personal indulgence, and every other visit may be applied to those in purgatory." What said the greatest controvereialist the Romish Church ever had—Cardinal Bellarmine ? "No man can be certain with the certainty of faith that he has a true sacrament, since the sacrament is not formed without the intention of the minister, and no one can see the intention of another." The Dublin" Irish Times" of March 22 last, gives some particulars of the will of John Fegan, in which he be- queaths fourteen hundred pounds forillasses at five shil- lings each for the eternal repose of his soul and the souls of his wife and child, &c. Poor deluded dupe! A policy of priestcraft to keep the people in darkness. ROBERT FOULKES.
Frodsham, May 6, 1890.
G. W. IIARGRE.AVES. Horsforth, near Leeds, April 23, 1890.

A FEW MORE FACTS ON ROMAN CATFIOLICISM. quite agree with Mr. Wilkinson where he says that "We must study the bible, and get at the true meaning of the Word of God." But how are we to re- concile this excellent advice of Mr. Williamson's with a letter written by Pope Leo XII. to his elerg,y on the occa- sion of his advancement to the papal throne on the 3rd of May, 1824? It was printed by the printer and book- seller to the Royal College of St. Patrick, Maynooth, and publisher to the Roman Catholic bishops of Ireland. In it he says, "You are aware, venerable brethren, that a certain society, called the Bible Society, strolls with effrontery through the world; which society,contemning the traditions of the Holy Father, and contrary to the well-known decree of the Council of Trent, labours with all its might, and by every means,to translate, or rather, to pervert the Holy Bible into the vulgar languages of every nation ; from which proceeding it is greatly to be feared, that what it is ascertained to have happened as to some passages, may also occur with regard to others ; to wit, that by a perverse interpretation, the Gospel of Christ be turned into a human gospel ; or what is still worse, into the gospel of the devil." Mr. Wilkinson up- braids us with being bigoted. I wonder what he thinks of Leo XII. speaking in this manner of a society which has published scores of millions of copies of the Word of God in shout 300 languages and dialects? But the Pope goes on to say "Behold then, venerable brethren.the tendency of this Society, which, moreover to attainits ends, leaves nothing untried ; for not only does it print its translation but also wandering through our town and cities, it delights in distributing them amongst the crowd. Nay, to allure the minds of the simple, at one time it sells them, at another with an in- sidumis liberality it bestows them." The Irish Roman Catholics prelates publicly avowed their full concurrence with the Pope's views, and charged their flocks to sur- render to the parish priests all copies of the Scripture re- ceived from the Bible Society. • When the Pope wrote his letter he, no d-iubt had in mind the following decree issued by the Council of Trent in their fourth session :—" Inasmuch as it is manifest from experience, that if the Holy Bible. translated into the vulgar tongue, be indiscriminately allowed to every- one, the temerity of men will cause more evil than good to arise from it, it is, on this point, referred to the judg- ment of the bishops, or inquisitors, who may by the advice of the priest or nonfessor, permit the reading of the Bible translated into the vulgar tongue by Catholic authors to those persons whose faith and piety, they ap- prehend, will be augmented and not injured by it; and this permission they must have in writing. But if any- one shall have the presumption to read or possess it without such written permission, he shall riot receive absolution until he have first delivered up such Bible to the ordinary. About noon on Monday, aftei the magisterial proceed- ings in the Town Hall, Richard Brierley, son of Mr. R. Brierley, the surveyor, had occasion to reach some docu- ments from the top of a small cupboard in Mr. Brierley's private office, where the attempt had been made to enter the safe. These articles were handed over to the police authorities, and in the afternoon Police Sergeant Long- worth, and Mr. R. Brierlesernade a thorough examination of the office, and snore burglariotre-looking implements were found on the tops of cupboards, as if they had been thrown or placed thereon in a great hurry. The articles included a wooden xnallat bearing a large number of marks corresponding with the heads of chisels iound on the Thursday ; an iron hammer the head of which was muffled with washleather, well worn, another key and two more pick-locks. THE COMMISSIONERS AND TFIE ROBBERIES. At the monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Commissioners, on Monday afternoon, the Surveyor (Mr. R. Brierley) referred to the offices having been broken into. He said: As you all know, gentlemen, a burglary has been committed on our premises, and money to the extent of .£l4 or £l5 has been taken. In addition to that the strong room of the Commissioners has been penetrated, and in another quarter of an hour it would have been entered and £l3O stolen. An iron safe must be obtained and fixed in the strong rootn.—Mr. Gillespie moved that Mr. Brierley be empowered to get quotations from different safe makers and report to the Board at the next meeting. He remarked that the room which had been termed the strong room was, in fact, a perfect farce. It was a delusion, and anyone with a strong pair of shooting boots could kick it through. He was sur- prised it had not been tampered with before,. aed to keep valuable papers and cash there was as perfect farce.— Mr. Forster : It is a nine-inch wall.—Mr. Gillespie:There is nothing to prevent any man getting in in ten minutes. —The motion was carried unanimously. PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. AT WARRINGTON. The prisoner was brought up at the County Petty Ses- sions at Warringtore on Wednesday, before Messrs. S. Rigby and J. Tinsley, when he was committed to take his trial at the Quarter Sessions to be next held at Liver- pool. He was defended by Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens. He was first charged with having broken into and entered the Town Hall, at Newton, sometime between 5 o'clock on the afternoon of the 30th April and the morn- ing of theist May, and stolen therein five florins. MR. BRIRRLEY'S. EVIDENCH. Richard Brierley, surveyor and clerk to the Newton Improvement Commissioners, deposed that he lived at Crow-lane. Newton, and had an office in the Newton Town Hall. Prisoner was formerly in his serve*, but left his employ about July, 188 R. Prior to then he had been a clerk in witness's office for twelve years. When he left he said that he was going into the service of the I Reddish Local Board as school attendance officer and assistant surveyor. In the Town Hall, at Newton, the Commissioners had a board-room at the top of the stairs, on the left. Witness had missed various sums of money at different times, extending over the period ot the last three months. The money. missed had been planed .in a private drawee,. In witness's private office. He recently marked five florins. On the Wednesday previous witness saw the coins safe in a drawer, which he locked. At about four o'clock on , the morning of the Ist May, witness was.called up by al messenger from the police, and went to the. Town Hall. He there saw the prisoner, who was in euetedy of Ser. geaet Longworth and Constable Spencer. Witness ex- amined the state of his office and drawer, and found that the drawer was open and the marked money was gone. The desk had been pulled out from. against the wall into the middle of the room. The desk had been against the wall of the strong room. The wall had been hacked and cut away, and a hole had been partly, made through 'it. Some of the implements produced were lying near the hole, including a candle, a chisel, and a saw. Later on the same morning, the police showed witness the five florins produced, which he recognised as the coins that he had put into his drawer; he recognised them by the marks he had put on them. Witness had also missed keys from his office drawers; two of the keys produced were similar to the ones he had missed. One of the keys would unlock the drawer of the money box, but it was now bmken.-11s, Mr. Swift : Prisoner left witness's employ of his own accord, with a good character, and witness gave him a testimonial. Prisoner had been back in Newton for some time. When prisoner was in witness's service he had to receive rnoney,and witnese had always found him strictly honest.—By the Clerk ; mere was a large sum of money, in the strong room at the time when it was broken into. THE CAPTURE BY TM POLICE. Constable Spencer, stationed at Newton-le-Willows, said that on the 30th April, at 11.30 pm, he went to the Town Hall at, Newton, to watch the place, ia consequence of robberies having been committed in the building. That was the twentieth night he had been watching there. At 11.45 witness heard the side door of the Town Hall open, and heard someone enter. The door was then locked, and the person who had entered went up to the relieving officer's room. Witness heard the door of that room opened, and the person then came out again and went to Mr. Brierley's office, upstairs. The constable saw him go into Mr. Brierley's room. Two or three minutes afterwards he heard a noise in Mr. Brierley's back office, as of sawing and hammering, and occasionally as though sense heavy piece of furniture was being dragged along the floor a the room. Shortly before two o'clock Ser- geant Longworth came to the window, and, after witness had communicated with him, also came into the building. The two policemen, in company, watched outside the door of Mr.Brierley's room until a quarter to four o'clock. During the whole of the time thus occupied they heard hammering going on inside the room. At about a quar- ter to four prisoner opened the door cautiously, and they at once recognised him. When prisoner saw witness he banged the door to again. With the assistance of the sergeant witness managed to get his staff between the door and the door-posts, but the prisoner wedged the door fast by means of a chisel, thus hindering their entrance. After they had forced the door open they ermine that the prisoner had escaped into the back office and barricaded the door, to which was attached spring lock. The sergeant requested the prisoner to open the door, but he refused. i They consequently broke the panel n, and then the prisoner said " I will surrender." Fie was taken into custody. Upon searching the prison Fr witness found 28 keys, two wire pick-locks, a pair of pliars, and a trowel. These articles were produced. Mr. Brierley, who was now present, spoke to the prisoner, and said "Why do not you turn the money up, or say where it is." Prisoner Said, "I know nothing about it. Ido not know where it is. I want to speak to you, Mr. Brierley. I want to tell you what I was going into the safe for. I have

applied for a situation at Flint, and wanted to ,get theseal of the Commissioners to attach to a testimonial." Wit- ness then took prisoner tothe poliCestation, and charged him with breaking into and entering the Town Hall. Prisoner replied—" Not guilty as far as theft." Witness then went to the prisoner's house, in company with [ Sergeant Longvrorth, and made a search. On the dressing-table in the prisoner's bedroom they found some money, Including five fiorM pieces, which Mr. Brierley identified as his property.—Sergeant Longworth gave evidence in corroboration of the statement of the con- stable.

Mn. SWIFT SPEARS FOR THE DEFENCE. Mr. Swift then addressed the Bench on behnif of the I prisoner. He hoped, he said, that they would deal with the case summarily, and not send his client for trial. It was unfortunately perfectly clear that the prisoner had committed felony in taking money belonging to M. Brierley, bubthey must take into consideration his pre- vious good character. With regard to the theft there was undoubtedly SO legal defence, and no moral defence. That was the prisoner's first offence, and his friends had expressed much astonishment and regret that he had committed the act lie had, and could urge no reason for his having done so. He had lived in Newton all his life. He had applied for a, situation at Flint, and left his place under the Reddish Local Board because he did not care for the duties, but the means he took to obtain the seal' the Commissioners were decidedly improper, and absolutely without justification. The only, reason his friends could urge in extenuation was that at the time he committed the offence)* was not master of himself. The Bench had power, under the First Offenders' Act, to inflict a fine, or commit prisoner for a term not exceed- ing six months. The magistrates then retired to consider the case, and an their return the Chairman, Mr. Rigby, said that they had given careful consideration to the defence, but they felt that the onus was too great for them to deal with the case summaiily. Prisoner was then committed to answer the charge at the next Q,liarter Sessions.

THE CHARGE OF STEMUNO DOCUMENTS. Caldwell was then further charged with having stolen, from the office of Mr. Brierley,, some time before the Ist May, eight bundles of plans drid dckuments, and four books, of the value of £3, the property of the Newton Improvement Commissioners. Mr. Brierley stated that he had an of4ce at the Town I Hall, in which, he transacted son,* of his own business, as well as that of the Commissioners. Prisoner was em- ployed as a cl&k in the office until 1888. The books, plans, Srci, produced, were the property of the Commis- sioners, and wera kept by witness as, their clerk. He had from timeto time missed the hooks and plans. He first missed them about two years ago. Some of the plans and spectheations were his own property. On Thursday morning witness, in company with Sergeant Longworth, went to the prisoner's house, and on a search being made, the • articles mentioned were found in a portmanteau in prisoner's bedroom. They were valued at 23. Sergeant Longworth corroborated, and added that when charged with this offence, prisoner replied, "I did not steal them ; I only took them to get copies." Prisoner was committed for trial on this charge also.

div.head: SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL
RUNCORN.

• There are signs that work on the Runcorn Section will shortly proceed more briskly than has been the case for the past few months. Piling operations are being carried on near Old Quay preparatory to constructint,° the lock. by which vessels from Widnes may enter the canal. Lower down, near Runcorn Bridge, mud and sand are being scooped out of a coffer dam, 'presumably so that the work a constructing the concrete wall ef the canal may be continued. Opposite the pumping station, there is also a pile driver at work, making the dams necessary for the construction of the lock that is to allow vessels to enter into Runcorn Docks. As yet the number of men employed on the section are very few. THE SHIP CANAL BRIDGES AT LATCHPORD. A HIGH LEVEL BRIDGE ADOPTED.

The subject of the bridges to cross the Ship Canal at : Latchford was again before the Daresbury Highway Board on Thursday. The subject was introduced in a letter from Mr. Leader Williams, the chief engineer of the canal undertaking, who stated that the Company's : engineers would wait upon the Board with amended plans. The Chairman (Mr. T. C. Parr) said he knew the "Various Powers Bill" of the Canal Company had been put back in Parliament, but it would have to come for- ward again soon. The Company had certain modifica- tions in their plans to show which they were in hopes would induce the Board to alter to a slight extent the : decision come to before. Mr. T. Hall asked if the plans that were to be again submitted proposed the abandonment of Acker's- lane swing bridge. .The Chairman believed they involved that. Mr. Leader Williams had spoken to him on the subject in London, but he told him that, unless they proposed something that the Board could go into, it was useless coming before it again. Mr. Jn. Darbyshire said the matter was being again brought forward in face of the unanimous resolution of the Board. The Chairman, said that was a new Board, and he thought they might approach the subject with their minds open. It was a question which involved the interests of a very large part of Cheshire. Mr. T. Hall said that that subject had already been voted tupon no fewer than four times, and it had been before the Committee six times, and yet they were still told to approach the questein with their minds open. He had acted in favour of what he thought would be for the benefit of the many as against the few. It was quite true that those who could drive their carriage and pair would have no objection to. the high level bridge, but he thought those who could not do that would have a great objection. He considered that matter was being brought before the Board in a personal and indecent manner, and he had come in contact with people who said they were surprised at the manner in which that question was being repeatedly brought be- fore the Board. The Chairman hoped that what Mr. Hall said about the personal bearing of the matter did not apply to him (the chairman). He VMS there as their chairman, and he should take a neutral position in the matter, though his opinions were well known. It W4B then decided to call the Canal Company's engineers (Mr. Hunter and Mr. Brooks) into the room. These gentle- men then explained the proposals they had to lay before the Board. They included a swing bridge 38 feet wide at Knutsford-road, and a swing bridge of the same width at Stockton Heath, the abandonment of the swing bridge 'at Ackers-lane, and the sunstitutim of a high level vehicular bridge near Latchford station. The gra- dients of the approaches to this high level bridge would, Mr. Hunter stated, be nowhere steeper than one in 25. It was also stated by Mr. Hunter that it had been definitely decided that the Latchford goods station was to be on the high level. If their proposals were adopted by the Board, the Canal Company would under- take to construct a new road along the south bank of the canal from the Northwich-road at Stockton Heath 0 Acker's-lane, and also to straighten the Northwich-road at Wilderspool. Mr. Hunter stated that a person on the south bank of the canal at Ackers-lane, would, if he went down Ackers-lane and up linutsford-road, have to traverse a distance of 244 D yards before he reached War- rington Bridge. If he went by the proposed new road to Stockton Heath, and thence by Wilderspool Causeway to Warrington Bridge, the distance would only be fifty yards more, namely 2,490 yards It was pointed out that, if the new road from Stockton Heath was made, there would be a continuous road along the south bank of the canal from the Chester-road at Lower Walton nearly to Thelwall, with the exception of the short stretch in front of Mr. Gaskell's house at Latchford. This part, - Mr. Hunter said, would no doubt he completed at some : future time. After the Ship Canal engineers had retired from the Board rndm, Mr. J. L. Jones moved - that the Company's proposals be accepted by the Board. Mr. J. Parr seconded this proposal. Mr. W. Long said he had hitherto inen a strong opponent of the Company's pro- posals, but he thought they had now met the Board in every possible way, and he supported the proposal. Mr. T. Hall could see no reason why the Board should stultify itself, and he moved that the resolution passed at the last meeting in favour of the retention of Ackers-lane swing- bridge be adhered to. Mr. J. Derbyshire seconded this proposal. On a vote being taken there were nine in favour of adopting the Ship Canal Company's prop seal, involving the abandonment of Ackers-lane swing-bridge and the erection of a high level vehicular bridge, and four against. The proposals were therefore adopted.

div.head: SHIP CANAL MYSTERY.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL MYSTERY.

The adjourned inquest as to the death of the man Ellaman, who was found shot on the Ship Canal at Hollins Green, was fixed to be held yesterday, but it has been again adjourned till next Friday. Stren- uous efforts have been made by the police to find the whereabouts of the suspected man, Vaughan, but without success. Among the steps taken by the police has been the circulation of full descrip- tions of the missing man, and also copies of his photograph.
The Prince of Wales on Wednesday opened the Royal Military Exhibition at Chelsea Hospital, the object of which is to provide an increased number of soldiers' Institutes.

DISASTER ON THE OHIO RIVER. TWELVE LIVES LOST. NEW YORE, TrIERSDAY.—A crowd of people 'returning from a base-ball match at Wheeling, on the Ohio river, overcrowded the naphtha ferry boat, by which the river is crossed. The naphtha tank was upset, and the engineer was unable to control the vessel, which dashed into a barge and was overturned. Eighteen persons were sucked by thecurrent under the barge, :and twelve of them were drowned. Two of these were prominent citizens of the State.

A woman, named Charlton, the wife eft a customs officer, living in Garmoyle-st., Liverpool, on Thursday night murdered her three tchiklren,.a.ged four years, two years, and nine months, by, cutting., their throats with a razor. The woman alsb ,cut her, own thcoat. She is still alive, but in a precarinus condition.. On Sunday last Charlton-remarked to a neighbour that his wife was in A rather, despondent condition, but he thought she would be better in a day or two. hequiries show that when Charltomarrired;hetne theme wassome delay before the door was; opened by his wife-, who, immediately she saw hirbv, began to ha.clyutt her throat with a razor. The latest details are as. hillewstr—lt appears that Charles Arthur Charlton, wbotis employed as a clerk in the Customs, came home to thebouse, I 6 Garmoyle- road, to the soutlref the cemetery,.. Having waited fbr some minutes, he knocked again, and at last the door was. opened to him by his wife, who to hie-horrer held: a razor in her , hand, and was, bleeding prettzsely-from the throat. In a frantic state he ran to a neighbour,. who came back I with him to the house, and' on making a search they I found the three children dead 'with: their throats cut also. I Crowds then began to asserableten a field which extends between Ossmovle-rd. and 'the, railway line. Only one side of the-road has been built,. and that quite recently, so that the thoroughfare is-an excluded situation. Not- withstanding this, tl*people.,, who stood in groups, and circulated all kinds.of rumours,, continued to hang about until after midnight. At men yesterday :the mother, though in a weak state, VMS pregres.sing as,,well as. could be expected. BY AN OCCARIONAL CORMRSPONDENT. A curious incident occurred at Runcorn Docks, a day or two ago. After the traffic had been cleared away on the noon tide, it was found impossible to close the gates of the tidal basin, through some ob- struction at the bottom, A diver was sent down, and he discovered that the gates were clogged with what he thought was a ships "fender, and he attached a rope to it. An attempt was made to haul the obstruction to the surface, but it slipped off and as it was swept away by the ebb side, it was seen to be a fish about six feet long, and like a sturgeon in appearance. Having been crusher) be- tween the gates the fish was of course dead, bat it is believed to have been alive when: it first entered Runcorn waters, Last summer a couple of salmon were•caught opposite Widnes Ferry;. and it would seems that either the water is becorsing more purc.,. or that thelinny tribe are becoming, acclimatised, to the complicated nastiness of therlver. It is more probable: that the poor things lost their way, after "tippling hi the sm.' Speaking of the. Docks remind me that trade at -the port has been exceptionally brisk; during the past three months-;: in fact a busier period!was never known in the history a the port. The ship Canal contract is-responsible to a considerable, extent for this improvedtratte:. I the is hereby given that JOHN DOLBY, ESQUIRE, e District AUditor.forthe North Western Counties Audit District, has appointed the AUDIT OF THE ACCOUNTS OF THE COUNTY COUNCIL for the County of Cheifter, and of the County Treasurer and other Officers of such Council, for the year ended 31st day of March. 1890, to commence on MONDAY, the 19th day of May. 1890, at ten o'clock in the forenoon, at the Castle of Chester. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN, that a copy of such accounts duly made up and balanced, together with all account books, deeds, contracts, accounts, vouchers, and receipts mentioned or refei red to in such accounts will be deposited in my office, No. 41, Northgate-Bt..
